It would mean $55 per capita in the province of Quebec. Any insurance company, or all the private insurance companies together, would give the citizens of Quebec a full insurance plan including medical care, drugs, operations, all that for approximately $30 per capita, in the province of Quebec, which would represent savings of $25 per Quebec citizen.
Mr. Chairman, all this shows that private enterprise is still the most logical and the cheapest way to grant services to the Canadian people, as long as they have the means to finance that plan or the plan they choose.
Mr. Chairman, not so long ago, that is on April 20, 1965, the former minister of National Health and Welfare, now the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), said this before the members of the Optimist Club at Niagara Falls. I quote:
Under the Canada Assistance Plan-
I would change the word "assistance" which smacks too much of poverty, of public difficulties, and say instead "the right to live" of each individual.
-we are willing to match, dollar for dollar, the present provincial outlays in the field of allowances to mothers, assistance to those mothers who have dependent children.
We are willing to share the cost of health services given by the provinces to the recipients of assistance.
The minister said this, but what the people did not know, and what we must tell them, is that we have a bureaucracy to pay here in Ottawa, and also another bureaucracy to pay in Quebec. We pay two administrations for exactly the same thing, which means a multiplication of expenses and a division of services or a subtraction in respect of the needy.
The hon. minister added:
We will take steps to include the costs of medical, nursing, dental, optical and pharmaceutical care.
However, it will be for the provinces to decide on the scope of such services and they will be responsible for taking measures to provide the health services they consider best adjusted to their particular case.
This health legislation is interim legislation, which will be in operation only until the coming into force of a medicare scheme, which I hope will be very soon.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the government should get together around a round table with the responsible authorities and
March 8, 1966

Supply-Health and Welfare officials of the medical associations in Canada, with provincial officials, as well as the executives of existing companies in the country and in our provinces, in order to establish the cost of a medicare plan, under which the government would pay premiums to families, as well as to single persons, so as to insure the whole Canadian population.
Mr. Chairman, no one ever thinks of meeting with the heads of insurance companies, medical bodies and the provinces to discuss the best objective means of providing services and giving results to the Canadian family, to the private individual in Canada. Instead, we think of setting up plans and, when those plans are conceived in the government services, we think of other plans to adjust those that are not always adequate. And it is because of all those plans that we drum in each other's head that we end up in the situation we are now.
Mr. Chairman, the people are not asking for plans, they want results. The worker, the farmer, the miner are not asking the government to draw up plans for them. Workers, farmers, miners, journeymen, people in all classes of society are asking the government to provide the private individual with the financial help that will enable him to choose and set up his own plan in a country that could truly be called democratic.
Mr. Chairman, such plans have been presented at every session. This year there is medicare, called for by the members of the C.C.F party, the Canadian socialists, for 25, 30 and even 35 years. All sorts of plans are demanded by people who want the government to dominate the individual, the human being.
Mr. Chairman, as I said last night, we have asked for higher family allowances in Canada. We have increased the allowances of the members of the house and the senators, and so on, but we cannot increase the revenue of Canadian citizens, and yet it is the taxes paid by farmers and all classes of society that enables us to vote increased allowances for members of parliament and senators.
Mr. Chairman, as I said last night, we are not opposed to larger salaries for members of parliament, because the cost of life has increased; but it has increased not only for members of parliament but also for mothers of Canadian families.
Ask a Canadian mother about it; the hon. ladies who sit in this house are surely aware that it costs more today to clothe, feed and

house a child properly than it did 20 or 25 years ago. Conditions should be adjusted according to the times, according to 1966 rather than 1945.
In 1965-66, family allowances cost $599,500,000 to the government and the Canadian people; those are the estimates now under consideration and we hear ministers say it is costing too much, when the administration costs only of that department exceed $500 million and when $1,185 million are paid in interest on the national debt, that is, more than twice the amount paid in family allowances. This is the tribute paid for the financing but nobody is heard protesting against such a situation.
When a claim is being made for Canadian children, the cry of inflation, of demagogy goes up, the masses are being called to rise against lawful authority.
Mr. Chairman, there is no question of rising against anything, but we want to put the facts straight, pass laws according to human rights; and the most elementary justice requires that we give to human beings, to Canadians, so that democracy can survive, if there is any meaning in the word, so that we have a government of the people, by the people and for the people, and no longer a government for finance, of finance and to serve finance.
Let us start to serve the Canadian people and we will thus discharge the duty for which we were sent to the parliament of this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a few points in this afternoon's discussion of the estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare. First of all, I should like to speak on a problem which is related to physical fitness, a matter which I believe has been given considerable attention by the department, and to raise a problem which has been brought to my attention from within my constituency, but which I am sure is a problem in many other parts of the country too. The problem relates to amateur sport, and this might be the time to reiterate the demand for a study of amateur sport in this country.
There are many facets to this complicated problem. Some of them have been raised earlier in connection with the national sport of hockey, but there are also a great variety of matters which I think the Department of
March 8, 1966

National Health and Welfare probably should investigate.
One particular problem is the question of the increased expense incurred by amateur athletes in attempting to compete in amateur athletic events across the country. These events increasingly are becoming the preserve of the wealthy, or else demand a tremendous local effort in order to send athletes to such competitions.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I had, for example, a letter from Vernon, dated February 11, regarding a rather outstanding athlete in the constituency. The boy, Steven Lattey, referred to in the letter last year was Canadian national junior skiing champion. This week end he has been invited to participate in an international ski meet at Banff. Next week he is to fly east to defend his junior championship and participate in a ski meet at Quebec City. All these trips are at his own or his parents' expense. I suppose he could simply give up and not represent the west in the beautiful province of Quebec. However, we do have these sporting events that are competitive on a national scale. A severe problem exists in getting to the places where these events are held, particularly for the individual athlete whose sport does not have spectator appeal or the resources that more highly organized team activities have.
I have noticed a one-shot effort along this line to be made in the centennial year, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of January 21, under the centennial commission's program for school fitness tests in 1967. A whole variety of events has been lined up. The centennial commission is considering asking corporations to offer awards for outstanding achievement and the suggested award will be a $3,500 expense paid trip for 12 to 18 year old athletes to participate in the PanAmerican games. This is the sort of thing that should probably be put on a more continuing basis for the good of amateur athletics in the country. We should not be concerned only about what is going to happen in 1967 but also about what is going to happen throughout the following years. If some policy were worked out on the national level we might benefit and be able to participate in international meets to much greater effect than has been possible in the past.
The question of an investigation into amateur sports has been raised in connection with the game of hockey and the control that seems to be imposed by professional sport on amateur sport and on those taking part in the
Supply-Health and Welfare amateur sport from a very early age. I think this matter deserves serious consideration. I think the Department of National Health and Welfare might concern itself with the field of organized sport which is so constituted as to include children of extremely tender age. There is a warning in the March 5 edition of The Canadian in an article entitled, "The Big Machine That Runs Kids' Hockey". I recommend that article to the minister and his staff. The aspects covered in it could well be considered from the point of view of the health of children of tender age who are involved in what is a highly organized game which demands tremendous physical output and which has a high injury risk and a great deal of nervous strain. I wonder whether the department should not seriously be considering studies of the effects of such highly organized team sports when they involve six year old children and in which the most intense competition is encouraged. The age level is becoming lower and lower. I should think there might be real danger to the health of these children from such a sport not only at the time but also later in life.
It may be worth while looking into the cumulative effects of these sports in relation to the health of very young children who participate in extremely active sports. These sports might even be worth looking at from the viewpoint of the diversion of public funds into the very expensive and complicated facilities that are necessary for the numbers of very small children who participate in them. Frequently expensive facilities are necessary for children of tender age. When there is such a crying need for housing for the aged there may be a danger of too much public money being diverted to what is a more immediately popular use for the money. This too might be a question that could be studied by this department.
I should also like to raise an issue about the construction of homes for the aged. I have in mind particularly a home for the aged in my constituency. I do not think we would deny the need that exists for these homes. The home I refer to was built privately on the initiative of a person who is of very advanced age, an age at which many people have completely given up making any worthwhile contributions and are subsisting on welfare assistance from the government. Through the initiative of this individual a retirement home for 50 senior citizens was constructed. Unfortunately the building was subject to the imposition of the 4 per cent
March 8. 1966

Supply-Health and Welfare sales tax on construction materials, a tax which has since risen to 11 per cent, which again shows the evil aspects of the tax. It discourages the very type of construction we would most like to encourage.
Some provisions were made for exemption from this tax on certain types of construction. However, on application for the exemption it was discovered that this home for the aged did not qualify because to qualify it would have had to be in receipt of aid annually from the government of Canada or from a province for the maintenance of persons specified in the preceding subparagraph of the provisions. Unfortunately for this institution it is not receiving a regular grant from the province although it is receiving from the municipality in lieu of taxation something in excess of $4,000 each year. There is therefore a grant from one level of government which happens in this case to be the wrong level of government. The Excise Tax Act specifies that there can only be provincial participation in this sort of thing. I think that the federal department in conjunction with the provincial department might well consider allowing participation at the municipal level.
When the Act speaks of aid being received from the government of Canada for this sort of endeavour the words are misleading because apparently there is no aid at that level. The only effective aid which is covered is that given by a province. It would make much more sense to remove the words "government of Canada" from the Act and speak instead of a province or municipality so that one block to the construction of housing for the aged could be removed.
Finally I should like to say a word regarding the issue of medicare about which a great deal has been said. I am afraid I shall have to disagree with my friends to the right who last night urged the government to make sure it stood very firm on the four principles enunciated.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Considering the remarkable retreats we have witnessed in the last few days I am sure it would not be at all difficult for the government to abandon the compulsory features of its medicare proposal or to consider a provincial scheme to be adequate in the absence of compulsory features. Several of the provinces have gone ahead and developed medicare schemes and it seems to me it is now too late for the federal government to insist on one monolithic compulsory scheme if it turns out there is opposition from the provinces and if

the schemes which the provinces have instituted seem to be providing the extent of medicare which the people living in those provinces demand at certain times. We have become enraptured by the possibilities of a welfare state to the extent that "universal" and "compulsory" have become words of high praise, words which would seem in the minds of some people absolutely essential in the description of any scheme which might be considered worth while.
We know that the medical profession is not at all pleased about the suggestion that there should be a compulsory scheme. We know that a medicare scheme can succeed only with the co-operation of this most important group. I feel that the government in its negotiations with the provinces should consider carefully the desirability of taking any action in the area of medicare. I notice that in the words chosen to refer to medicare in the Speech from the Throne there seems to be a certain softening in the attitude initially taken by the government and I urge very strongly that the government should not insist on the one feature which would make medicare a source of intense dissension throughout the country rather than an area in which federal-provincial co-operation would provide the people of Canada with the degree of social assistance which they feel they can afford at this time. I believe it is quite possible for the federal government to work out the problem of providing for portable benefits without making the scheme monolithic and without making it compulsory.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief because I know what I am talking about.
May I rise to speak during the review of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare not to criticize but just to bring forward recommendat;ons which could be implemented if they were deemed useful after consideration. However, I will point out that if the provinces, in the course of their history, have decided to divide health and welfare into two different departments it is because thorough stud es on the subject have shown this was required by the increased responsibilities and administrative burden.
The last province to follow suit was Manitoba, in 1961, which, for the reasons already outlined has divided its department in two. If we consider the development of the Department of National Health and Welfare before the merger, in 1944, we see that it was
March 8, 1968

not a department, but a health branch which came successively under the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Department of Immigration and the Department of Commerce and Industry.
Only in 1919 and at the request of the Canadian Medical Association did the department become the Department of Public Health.
In 1929, the Pensions and Civil Re-establishment Division had become less important and a Pensions and National Health Division was created. Later, following the introduction of social security programs such as old age pensions and family allowances, related in a way to para-medical problems, the Department of National Health and Welfare was set up in 1944.
Since then, Mr. Chairman, other extensive programs were added to those already administered by the department, such as hospital insurance and several national health grants. Very soon the department will also be responsible for drawing up and implementing the national medicare program and the Canada assistance plan, not to mention the Canada pension plan which is already operative.
For those reasons, the Department of National Health and Welfare should be divided into two distinct units, so that we could reorganize the whole administrative framework. When you consider also the tremendous expenditures this department expects to make to carry out its future programs, I do not think there is any other way than the one I have just mentioned. First, this would make it possible to do away with administrative routine which, when it becomes too heavy, tends to bog down and thereby ceases to advance.
Then, this would give the departments more leeway for adequate planning to provide them with greater administrative flexibility and to justify the old saying: to govern is to foresee.
We have long been bogged down in an administrative stagnation where new ideas, lest they result in small mistakes and failures, have been completely set aside, at the expense of normal progress.
Finally, that will be one of the very important recommendations of the royal commission on health.
I pay tribute to the Department of National Health and Welfare which, in 1965, developed
Supply-Health and Welfare the Canada pension plan, one of the most daring undertakings to date of the department.
Those sir, are the few remarks which I wanted to make and which are really a combination of findings and suggestions, in the best interests of Canada.
Let those who criticize when the government advocates a program such as the health insurance plan know that we are aware imperfections can slip in. But if we had to wait for the legislation to be perfect to introduce or pass it-and even then, there would be criticism-we would never have that type of legislation in Canada.
Only to the extent where time has polished them have laws become almost perfect as human standards go, and I ask all doctors throughout the Canadian nation, my colleagues, to try to understand and appreciate our breadth of views on what seemed, a few years ago, an unattainable dream: health insurance.
That is one proof that the government wants the state, here in Canada, to exist for the individual and not the individual for the state.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been impressed with the need for having these estimates passed but with the exception of one brief contribution on the transport estimates I have said nothing s.nce the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were before us. I say this because I believe it is absolutely necessary that certain things be said at this stage with regard to one of the most urgent problems facing Canada today. I refer to the question of old age pensions.
I am glad that the new minister and his assistant come from two provinces where this question is never far removed from the public gaze, which is the case also in my province and indeed, the other provinces. The urgency is great. A part of the problem is to provide security for the aged, to provide thousands of our people w.th the modern standard of comfort or well-being which they so desperately lack. The other part of the problem is the method by which we are going to pay our debt to those people who helped build this country, who helped create the standard of affluence which we know exists but in which they share so little. This is the double problem involved.
March 8. 1966

Supply-Health and Welfare
The old cannot wait. We must seek to provide food for the living rather than following the practice, as we do so often today, of providing flowers for the dead. Food for the living is something that should be provided in much greater abundance than we are providing it today, and it must be provided now.
I want to point out several milestones in connection with old age pension legislation. Believe it or not, very few hon. members can remember as I do the debates which took place in this chamber and the other place when the first old age pension legislation was introduced in 1927, over 40 years ago. Prior to that time there was only one way by which many hundreds of old people could get assistance or relief. That was by dragging their sons or daughters into court and having the court find to its own satisfaction that their sons or daughters were not able to support them. The old age pension legislation was the first federal social security legislation put on the statute books of Canada.
Those who know anything about my history will know I have a particular reason for being interested in that legislation and its evolution, because today I consider that first social security legislation has become a monument to the memory of one man. Many helped but increasingly it has become well known as his monument.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The
first old age pensions were very meagre indeed, $20 a month at the age of 70 with a means test, but even then it was recognized we were establishing a principle and this was the first milestone with respect to old age pensions. At that time we established the principle that the elderly were persons entitled in their own right to our consideration and not merely as appendages to their sons and daughters. Prior to that they were considered as appendages to their sons and daughters to be looked after on a basis of charity and good will. It was only when the indignities heaped on old people had become so great and the physical and mental suffer-ring so unbearable that we took that first step.
Some improvements were made to the legislation during the 1930's and 1940's but they were minor. Then in 1951 came the second milestone in old age pension legislation in Canada, the passage of the Old Age

Security Act which was universal in its application and gave the pension to everyone at age 70. The pension at that time was raised to the amount of $40 a month.
This afternoon in this chamber I heard a member regretfully wishing that universality not be incorporated into our medicare legislation. I reply that the feature of universality in old age pensions which we established in 1951 is one of the finest things we have ever incorporated into Canadian social security legislation because it established a new principle. In 1951 we established the principle that every person at the age of 70 should be entitled to receive a measure of security from the community, regardless of any other consideration.
Let me add further that we did not do that just as nice Nellies or do-gooders. We did it because it was essential to establish that new principle. The earlier principle was that the elderly were entitled in their own right to receive consideration and a measure of security, and that was advanced in 1951 when we said that when people reached the age of 70 they were entitled to receive a measure of security from the community for the rest of their lives not as charity but as of right.
Sociologists in the United States, despite the fact that that country has so much piecemeal social legislation, are now eyeing with tremendous interest the idea of universality which we built into our scheme in 1951. When I hear the idea being mooted that we should place old age pensions in categories and give some of them free and others on the basis of a needs test-this needs test is recognized by all old people as a means test of a more frightful variety-I can only hope the government will not go back on one of the things which a preceding Liberal government enacted when it provided a foundation for old age pensions, medicare and other forms of security.
The principle of which I speak had another reason behind its establishment. Technology had advanced to the point where we were able to establish it and in fact had to establish it. In 1951 we recognized that there were a great number of people who, because they had spent their lives working in a period when wages were low, had not been able to put sufficient money aside for their old age. We also recognized or at least we were getting it through our skulls, which as human beings are pretty thick, that if we were going to have constantly rising incomes, constantly
March 8, 1968	COMMONS
rising revenues and constantly rising production we had to find ways and means of distributing buying power among the population so that production would move out of the factories and could be sold, thus creating a demand for more production. All of us have not yet learned that lesson but we will learn it in a bitter way unless we learn it in a humane and wise way before it is too late.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Let there be no more of the argument that we are going to give the old age pension only to people who really need it, that we are going to scrutinize every case and will not give it to those who do not need it. On the matter of cost, when you have a whole army of social service investigators going around making these inquiries all the time the cost is very great. It is also useless and unnecessary. The social welfare people are getting fed up spending their time doing this instead of doing rehabilitation work and getting people back into a position where they can be self-supporting even if only to a certain extent. We are wrong in trying to do it in this way.
The most fair tax in Canada or anywhere else is the tax on income. I see no reason that we should not take the old age pension, old age security pension or whatever pension we are giving to elderly people, make it available to everybody at age 65 and then use the instrument of the income tax to take back according to the person's ability to pay. That is what the income tax can do and it is the fairest way of seeing that people pay their share of the cost of security across this country. If the government should have other ideas in mind, those of us in this party will want to take a long hard look before we are pushed off the solid rock of the income tax which is the fairest and the universal way of seeing that it is done justly and in a sensible way administratively as well.
I heard the hon. member for Villeneuve this afternoon talk about wasteful expenditures of one sort or another among governments. Let me suggest that one wasteful expenditure is the probing and digging into people's affairs by reasons of a means test and a needs test, quite apart from the indignity which is involved.
I should like to say also that there were increases in the old age security pension in the 1950's and 1960's. In 1957 it went up from $46 to $55. In 1962 an increase again in the old age security pension brought it up to $65. In 1963 it went up to $75. By this time the elderly people of Canada were beginning to
DEBATES	2367
Supply-Health and Welfare think that the only way they could get an increase in the pension was by having elections. Had I been on the old age pension I imagine I would have thought that an annual election was about the only way to try to catch up to the cost of living.
The cost of living has continued to rise. Because of the rising cost of living the older people have been dropping farther and farther behind. Let me point out what has happened since the last increase was given in 1963. The cost of living has gone up 5.4 per cent. With today's prices we would have to increase it to $79 even to make it equal to $75 in 1963. Something else has happened which we must not lose sight of. In this period the standard of living has been rising, wages and salaries have been going up, profits have been going up and income has been going up. When this has been happening the people on low fixed incomes have been falling farther and farther behind. The production of goods and services also has been going up. So merely increasing the pension rate a little bit, even to meet the cost of living, will not bring the old age pensioners up to the modern standard of living which they must have if we are going to do the job we should be doing at this time.
I say, Mr. Chairman, it is now time for a third milestone-1927, 1951, and now 1966. We are waiting to see whether the government proposes to make this year a milestone and the older people across the country are wading to see what is going to be done to make it a milestone. I am going to say categorically at this time that we should establish a new principle, the principle that every person at age 65 shall have the right to a pension which will provide a modern standard of living with neither a means test nor a needs test. I do not think we can do anything less than that. Certainly we have to fight for that with all the ability we have.
I am going to suggest now the things that we in this party, and I would like to hope members of other parties, feel must be embodied in this legislation when it comes in. First, I should like to say that it should be made a right and not a charity, that it become universal in Canada and that we give it to people from age 65. That is the first point.
Second, I wish to say that it must include neither a means nor a needs test which involves checking into the affairs of people, and an unwarranted interference with the older people. In the past this has been one of
March 8. 1966

Supply-Health and Welfare the reasons many of these people have tried their best to stay away from it as long as they possibly could. We hope that this pension will be given to everyone and that the surplus will be taken back in income tax according to their ability to pay.
The third principle is that the levels must be high enough to provide a modern standard of living. I know a general stand has been taken in support of the idea of pensions in the amount of $100 a month at age 65. I suggest the authorities have to reach the conclusion that that is not sufficient to provide a modern standard of living in the face of today's cost of living and standard of living. The committee which met in the other place suggested we should make the amount higher than $100 a month. They have suggested $105 a month for a single person and $185 a month for a couple.
As late as last fall the Toronto Metro Social Planning Council came to the conclusion after a careful study that for a minimum standard of living, health and decency the amount would have to be $126.47 for single persons and $213.02 for a couple. Last January, with the cost of living again having risen, the Conference on Ag ng met in Toronto and set up a sub committee of welfare people, social workers and experts in other fields. This subcommittee came to the conclusion that the amount for a minimum of health and decency should be $138.96 for a single person and $223.82 for a couple. These are figures which are given by competent and responsible people across this country.
I think it will be up to the government to consider these points carefully before it brings in its proposals. As I say, we must remember we live in a society where we can afford these things and where we must afford them if we are going to keep our production rising constantly. We must bring our ideas up to date. It is our ideas which are penurious and backward. I might point out that this is a much better type of national defence than all the bombers, battleships and bastions that we could possibly devise. This is the sort of thing we must do if we are to be strong economically in the modern world.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I now come to the fourth principle I suggest should be embodied in our legislation. I know some will suggest that this is a far-out suggestion, perhaps including some hon. members of the party to which I belong, but I think the time has come, and sociologists agree with me, to take the ceiling off earnings 
and other incomes of recipients of old age pensions. We talk constantly about creating incentives for people to save and be thrifty, incentives for people to go out and work while they can, rather than just sitting around until they become sitting ducks for doctors' offices and welfare workers. Why in the name of time can we not allow these old people to go out and perform baby sitting or the other part time jobs they can find in order that they may salt away a few dollars without being penalized? I have known of cases, as I am sure others have, where people have had to spend every last cent they had set aside for their funerals, as the welfare people express it, before being able to obtain supplementary assistance. I suggest it is time to do away with this kind of ox cart mentality, this penny-pinching line of thought that does not fit into our society today. This type of thing is economically a detriment rather than a help.
My fifth point is that pensions must be geared not only to the cost of living and made adjustable to that level but also to the rising standard of living that we enjoy. I am not going to take much more time but I want to refer to two or three people who live in my riding and the circumstances of their situations. I am sure hon. members could do the same in respect of older people living in their ridings.
In Vancouver there lives a couple aged 78 and 77 who are self-respecting people trying to get along on just their pensions. They attempted to obtain more but they were unsuccessful because one had $48 in a bank account and the other had a little more in a credit union. They were told they could not receive supplementary assistance until they had used that money and they decided to attempt to manage on $1,800 per year.
This couple is managing to get along on their pensions alone because they own their own house. They pay taxes of $84 per year which would be $184 were it not for the efforts of the provincial premier.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
You
may congratulate him, but let me tell you that he has been successful in this regard only by starving the municipalities.
The couple to whom I have referred pay $40 per year for insurance on the house, which is all they can possibly afford. They pay health insurance premiums of $60 per year. This would be cheaper if we had a
*March 8. 1966	COMMONS
universal health insurance plan. The old gentleman bought glasses last year which cost $32. He needs a dental plate very badly but cannot afford one. In January they both had the flu and his wife had to have a prescription filled at a cost of $6.50. I should like to know how any of us could manage to budget for two people with $1,800 per year. This couple manages to pay these fixed costs in a self-respecting way by cutting down to a diet *of bread and tea with precious little else.
This kind of treatment is not good enough for people of this quality or calibre, nor is it .good enough for another woman to whom I wish to refer who lives not in my constituency but in a small Ontario town. This woman writes in these terms:
My husband is 70 years old and we have to live on his pension. He is a very sick man with [DOT]emphasema, a form of asthma. Each month it cost him $25 and sometimes $30 for pills. I am *62 and not old enough for a pension. I can't work, my heart is very weak. We have to pay $35 rent and telephone $3.55-something we have to have in an emergency. Lights too are high.
There is something else that is high. That woman's courage is high. These people have precious little to work on but hope-hope long deferred. I am sure that every member of this house could cite cases exactly similar to the ones I have cited this afternoon.

Surely it is equally obvious in view of the positions that several provinces are now taking that the formula will have to be amended. I refer

Whenever someone such as the hon. member for Simcoe East suggests that there are areas of need in medical care such as more doctors, more medical schools, funds for the chronically ill and mentally ill, up go the smokescreens and we are treated to a heartrending story of how evil and debasing is the means test. If you were a widow on mother's allowance and needed more milk for your children, did you get it without this rigid and degrading means test? Consider my province of Saskatchewan. There we have a real paradox. Our patient-bed ratio is among the best in the world and yet we are faced with long hospital waiting lists. Even cancer patients have to wait months for a bed and some heart attack and fracture cases have been turned away because there are no beds for them. Imagine the situation at the University Hospital where for months complete wards are closed because of the critical shortage of nursing and other personnel. These situations have all existed; they are a matter of public record. Hospitals are faced with ever-increasing costs of operation but still there are not enough funds to provide some of the modern equipment that is considered to be so essential in running a hospital today. These are facts, Mr. Chairman, not fantasy but grim facts.
I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not turn out to be another of those who fail to see the situation in its true light and blunder on blinded by the brilliant beam of political opportunism. I sincerely hope he is not one of those. Suffice it to say that we must look very closely at these other areas of need in this country. I ask the

government to look again at the Hall Commission report wherein they point out that we need doctors and we need health resource funds immediately to start building in the next few years for the number of doctors and the other personnel that will be necessary at that time.

Mr. Chairman, if the present government often considers its administration with satisfaction, it happens, on the other hand, that millions of Canadians are unhappy about the huge sums of money spent on national defence and the complacency of the government with regard to the interest on the public debt.
Faced with poverty and increasing needs, those Canadians are asking the government to increase family allowances.
Supply-Health and Welfare
The Family Allowances Act was sanctioned on August 15, 1944 and went into effect on July 1, 1945. At the outset, the allowances decreased progressively with the number of children, but the government corrected that situation in 1949.
Apart from a small increase in 1957, the allowances have remained much the same until now.
Here is how the system works today. For each child under 16, the government pays $6 or $8 a month, according to the child's age. Under the terms of another act passed in 1964, that is the Youth Allowances Act, young people between 16 and 18 who are still going to school get $10 a month.
I wish to point out that since 1945, the allowances have hardly increased, whereas the cost of living went up sharply. As a matter of fact, between 1945 and 1965, the cost of living jumped by 87.7 per cent whereas family allowances increased by 9.4 per cent only.
Is it necessary to recall that in 1945, milk cost 8 cents a quart and bread 10 cents a loaf? We know that today, just to give a few examples, the price of milk has tripled and the price of bread has more than doubled. Those are undeniable facts.
Moreover, since 1945, our economic growth and our national production have increased considerably. Production increased not only in value but in volume and quantity.
I realize that each year the central government allocates huge amounts for family allowances. Thus, in 1965, Ottawa spent $550,571,248 for 6,849,095 Canadian children. We also know that since the fiscal year 1957-58 Quebec is no more the province which draws more allowances in this field, but Ontario.
If Ottawa already spends large sums in family allowances, one must not conclude that its contribution is sufficient. On the contrary, this question must be discussed considering not only the high cost of living but the families' limited income and acute needs.
I am thinking, for instance, of the situation of Quebec families. Mr. Jacques Henripin, a demographer and University of Montreal professor, drew the following outline in a lecture he delivered in November 1965 to the Family Social Services Federation congress:
Out of the 994,000 non-farm families, 18 per cent have an income lower than $2,500; 24 per cent have an income between $2,500 and $4,000; 29 per cent are in the $4,000-$6,000 bracket; and the remaining 29 per cent have an income higher than $6,000.
March 8, 1966=

Supply-Health and Welfare
Therefore, one finds, sir, that family needs, even though I choose only those of Quebec, as an example, become alarmingly greater.
That is why there is only one imperative solution and the initiative is a matter of urgency: the family allowances scheme must be amended without delay if hardship and poverty are to be fought effectively in this country.
At the last federal-provincial conference of Ministers of Health and Welfare in January 1966, the representatives of five provinces at least called for such a revision: those of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Newfoundland.
If Ottawa delays any longer, the provinces which will take action will not be to blame. Hon. Rene Levesque announced at that conference that Quebec would take action shortly in this field if the central government failed to do so.
Besides, it is to be wondered whether the administration of this program should not be entrusted to the provinces. Any province would then be free to set up within its boundaries a better comprehensive scheme including every aspect of social security.
It already seems as if the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) sees no objection to the provinces handling the distribution of family allowances. This attitude became apparent during an interview with parliamentary correspondent Charles Lynch over the English network of the C.B.C. on January 18, 1966.
It would seem, however, that the federal Minister of Health has no desire whatever that Ottawa should abandon the administration of family allowances.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I feel that this problem is under provincial responsibility, because it is an area touching upon social and educational fields. The constitution of 1867, in its spirit and in its wording mainly under chapters 92 and 93, gives the provinces exclusive jurisdiction over social and educational matters.
The fact that Ottawa entered this field of action in 1944 by not giving the provinces their fiscal revenue does not mean that the federal government was constitutionally empowered to do this.
It must be pointed out here that Ottawa passed its legislation on family allowances without first using a constitutional amendment. It proceeded differently with regard to unemployment insurance in 1940 and old age pensions in 1951.

In fact, the federal Family Allowances Act of 1944, as that of 1964, which provides for payment of allowances to children, in addition to dealing with social needs, constitutes indirect interference in the field of education, since a child must go to school in order to be eligible for the allowance.
Therefore, it would be to Ottawa's advantage-and it would have plenty of time to do it-to devote itself to the national and international matters specifically mentioned in the constitution and to hand back to the provinces the responsibility for and the administration of family allowances.
While waiting for that development to take place, since it is urgent to amend the system of family allowances, we must ask ourselves what should be the social philosophy behind such a change.
Family allowances are related to the essence of human dignity and social welfare. The state should especially encourage its younger citizens and support the family, which is truly the basic cell of society.
As the taxpayers supply the amounts of money the state distributes, it is fitting that, in this field, the plan should be universal, just as in the case of old age pensions, health insurance and superannuation plans.
However, it is fitting that we should consider various degrees and standards in its application. For instance, with regard to allowances, family needs can be catalogued. The extent of the needs shall be studied without discrimination. The number of children per family, their age, as well as the father's income, should to be taken into consideration. Allowances could be paid according to a realistic and selective scale.
On the basis of these general principles, one can imagine various family allowances schemes.
Whatever the scheme to be adopted by amending the present one, I suggest that the new formula should be comprehensive, in proportion with the number and the age of children, based on needs, not on the simple wish to increase buying power it should take into account the father's income and the increase in the cost of living and it should be accompanied by an adjustment or exemptions concerning income tax legislation.
The new plan, in spite of realistic features, should not eliminate the first child from the benefits. The first child cannot be set aside mathematically. This child does not choose his rank upon his birth and he is a citizen
March 8, 1966

like the others and he has needs; he often grows up in a needy environment and, later, he will pay taxes for thousands of other children. Consequently, any discrimination against the first born should be rejected.
It is understood that an early change to the family allowances program will increase government expenditure under the Department of National Health. But this increase, under National Health, could be compensated by reductions in other areas, by elimination of waste or by permitting the institution of a provincial lottery.
One fact stands out, in conclusion: The government must take measures to increase family allowances considerably and thus effectively fight poverty through a more equitable distribution of national income. Such is the fundamental requirement of a truly democratic government.

As a matter of fact, I thought it would be a very good idea if the statements of the hon. member for Saskatoon were drawn to the attention of the people of this country and particularly to the people of the province of Saskatchewan.
The first comment of the hon. member was that the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan took from 1944 to 1962 to set up medicare. If he was as well qualified as he pretends to be he would have told the committee that the C.C.F. government was elected in Saskatchewan in 1944 on a promise to set up, stage by stage, a comprehensive health insurance program. The medical care program even in 1962 did not constitute the final stage as it does not cover drugs, dental care, glasses or other ancillary services. The hon. member might have pointed out to the committee that one of

Supply-Health and Welfare the first things the C.C.F. government did in 1944, with a total provincial budget of a little over $30 million, was to set up completely free care for the mentally ill, both mental in hospitals and psychiatric clinics, followed by the first completely free cancer program covering treatment, deep X-ray therapy, surgery and post-operational care. The provincial government set up completely free health services for the first time in Canada for all assistance groups such as old age pensioners, those receiving mothers' allowances, wards of the government and blind persons.
The province set up in one health region the first completely universal medicare program for all residents of that region, some 65,000 persons, by way of a pilot project as early as July 1, 1945. That plan is still in operation. It provided the statistical data upon which the provincial plan could be based and also provided a good deal of the data which was of use to the Hall Commission. On January 1, 1947, the provincial government set up the first comprehensive hospital insurance program in Canada and on this continent. We in the provincial government made it very clear to the federal government, first Liberal and later Conservative, that if at any time they were prepared to pay a substantial part of the cost we would be able to proceed with comprehensive medicare.
It was not until 1961 that the province felt it had sufficient revenue to proceed with comprehensive medicare, because the entire burden of this program had to be borne by the provincial government. Therefore, for the hon. member for Saskatoon to suggest that there was any delay in implementing the promises of 1944 is either an attempt to mislead the committee or is a woeful betrayal of ignorance. Knowing the hon. gentleman, I can make my own selection.
The second matter he referred to was the question of means tests. He referred to the speech made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway and said that while the members of the New Democratic party decry means tests, nevertheless in the province of Saskatchewan under the C.C.F. government means tests were retained.
Means tests were retained under the Old Age Assistance Act which provides for a pension to be paid jointly, in part by the federal government and in part by the provincial government. The regulations are laid down by the federal government and under them the provincial government is required
March 8. 1986

Supply-Health and Welfare to impose a means test. We expressed our willingness at federal-provincial conferences, both under the Liberal federal government and under the Conservative federal government, to pay our share of the cost of the government would be prepared to remove the means test. The hon. member for Saskatoon has not pointed out that during the six years the Conservative government was in office the means test was retained and that there was no willingness on their part to remove it in spite of our repeated requests.
It is true that with reference to provincial programs a means test had to be retained, particularly with reference to supplementary pensions for the old age security group. It is also perfectly apparent that with the limited financial resources a provincial government has it is almost impossible to pay a universal pension to everyone at a certain age, because a provincial government does not have the power a federal government has of collecting back in income tax a substantial part of the pension from those who do not really require it.
I want the committee and the people of Saskatoon to notice that the hon. member is arguing for the application of a means test to medicare. Does this mean that the conservative party members have now become the exponents of means tests? Does this mean they propose that the old age security pension now universally paid should be rescinded and a means test applied? If a means test is fair and equitable in medicare, it is equally fair and equitable when applied to a pension. Is the Conservative party now, through its recent more reactionary acquisitions, announcing that it has taken the backward step of supporting means tests in social welfare and health problems?
I hope that Conservative members, particularly from Saskatchewan, who have campaigned a great deal on the question of removing the means tests, will now make it perfectly clear whether the hon. member for Saskatoon was speaking for the Conservative party and particularly for the Conservative members for the province of Saskatchewan.

The reason it is working is that the doctors are still dedicated individuals who are working hard to give the best possible care to their patients despite the fact that there is overutilization of their services, despite the fact that they are working much longer and much harder than they ever worked. But I am afraid that by reason of the amount of work they are doing they are working in less depth than they should be in medical practice, and these are things which must be considered by the committee and the government in any proposals for medicare throughout the country.

I do not want to delay the committee, Mr. Chairman, but may I just make two points. Reference was made to the free cancer program in Saskatchewan. First of all, I want to point out to the hon. member for Saskatoon that the free cancer program which had been set up by a Conservative government in 1932 or 1934, if I remember correctly, provided only for diagnostic services and not one dollar was ever paid out for cancer treatment or cancer surgery until a C.C.F. government was elected in the province and supplied the necessary funds for that purpose.
The hon. gentleman also made reference to the fact that the hospitalization program was set up with not sufficient attention having been paid to the supplying of what he calls the distaff side. I suppose he means hospital equipment, plant and facilities. I would point out that between the time our government took office and the time the hospital insurance plan was established we doubled the number of hospital beds in the province. I have not looked at the figures for the last two years but for years Saskatchewan had the highest ratio of hospital beds per thousand of the population of any province in Canada and was only equalled by one state of the union, namely, the state of New York.
When the hon. gentleman points out that the medicare plan operating in Saskatchewan is not the same plan as proposed originally he
March 8, 1966	COMMONS
is really playing with words. The plan brought in did not outlaw private practice. That was the interpretation which was given it by certain persons who opposed the plan. It certainly was not concurred in by the law officers, but in order to satisfy any who might have fears in that regard, Premier Lloyd did agree to bring in amendments to the Act. But at the time the Act was introduced in the legislature I made it perfectly clear that our understanding and interpretation of the legislation, on the basis of opinions by the law officers, was that it left the medical profession the right, if they chose, to stay outside the plan.
I contend that the basic principle of having medicare available to each person, without requiring him to prove he is indigent or comes within a special category, has worked successfully, and I am convinced that if it is made applicable to all Canadians it will work equally well and be generally acceptable to the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) on his appointment to that post and I regret having to draw to his attention certain steps of doubtful value that were taken under his predecessor.


It could be that the former minister was not informed of the unwholesome work performed under his department's authority by certain medical doctors who probably wanted to justify their jobs and enhance their prestige before their friends.
In any case, those wretched individuals took advantage of the cow's product to cowardly bring honest citizens before the courts. Some farmers are now charged with having: put poor quality milk on the market. I am convinced that to force someone to stand trial, one must be sure that the accused is morally guilty. Therefore, in this case, the person who can honestly prove that the farmer is guilty, as far as the quality of the milk is concerned, is not yet born, for the very good reason that dairy milk is never bought but taken on consignment by the processors concerned. They go to the farmers to take delivery of the milk, they see to it that it is weighed and they only have the right to accept or return that product, and often, the product processed in several ways will be put on the market before the farmers get a penny.
At the present time, the dairy producers in the riding of Champlain are awaiting the verdict following a trial which took place before the courts in Trois-Rivieres.
Other farmers in my riding are awaiting their trial which has been set for March in Quebec City. It is through the R.C.M.P. that they learned that they had put milk of poor quality on the market on May 4, 1965. The farmers, who normally sell their milk $5.50 per cwt. get from their dairy a first, second and third notice when such a thing happens. Sometimes the farmers must stop delivering milf for a week or two, that is long enough to enable them to locate the trouble. But there is never any talk of a trial. However, in the case under consideration, that is dairy milk, for which the farmers get only $3 per cwt. when it costs them $3.50, there was not any first, second or third notice.
And what is most ridiculous about this situation, Mr. Chairman, is that the processor never stopped getting milk from those farmers.
I have here the quantities supplied by a producer for each day in 1965. They total 63,669 pounds. Either his product was good or it was not. If it was, the dairy did well to accept it. But if it was not, it might have been due to the herd which should have been killed. But it might have been due also to the refrigeration method. If the milk was considered unsuitable for making some products,

because it had been badly kept, the processor had the right and duty to refuse it; then, thousands of consumers would have been truly protected. The reputation of the farmers would not have suffered; and only a few lawyers would have in their pockets a few dollars less from the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The minister made a serious mistake when he mobilized the R.C.M.P. on Christmas eve to hand out summons to farmers throughout the province of Quebec, because around that time the same police officers might have focused their attention on Quebec City to prevent the distribution of thousands of pounds of meat from the United States which had been declared unfit for human consumption and, in addition, had been previously refused by the city of Montreal.
I ask the minister to look closely into this deplorable situation and to get in touch without delay with the farmers involved who are greatly concerned over what the future holds in store for them, because departmental employees who came to testify at the trial in Trois-Rivieres behaved in a manner which would please Fidel Castro very much.
We should not forget that there are in your department some employees who, for these same reasons, they obtained their job, could be somewhere else. This afternoon, just with a written charge, I could have any hon. member in this house locked up. I will not do it, because we live in a democratic country and mutual co-operation should rank before felony.

The first question is this: Mr. Chairman, it will be remembered that in 1963, his party, through the present prime minister, promised to extend student allowances to the age of 21.
It will be remembered that the former Minister of Justice, who now fills a high post in London, said to the house that the right hon. prime minister always kept his promises, and that he was giving himself four years within which to keep his promise to grant students allowances till the age of 21.
We would like the minister to tell us if he has had the opportunity, since he has become Minister of National Health and Welfare, to study the prime minister's promise, and to tell us when the government or himself expect to be able to grant these allowances to students until they are 21.
I ask that on behalf of the numerous Canadian families which see that family allowances have remained almost stationary since 1945.
If one compares the cost of living percentage points for 1945 with those of today, one sees that family allowances no longer meet the purposes for which they were granted in 1945.
I do not have figures here, this afternoon, but if my memory serves me correctly, the cost of living, according to the index set in 1949, was 100. In 1945, the cost of living would have been 75, according to the 1949 index. Today, we know that the cost of living increases very fast, particularly since the last two or three years. This means, Mr. Chairman, that if the government is ready to launch a war against poverty in Canada, the opposition is ready to support it.

Rene Levesque. But we have been hearing for many months that the hon. provincial minister intends to take over administration of family allowances. Would the hon. minister disclose the present stage of the discussions with Hon. Rene Levesque to this effect. I wish to point out that the statement of Hon. Rene Levesque to the effect that the first and even the second child of a family will not be covered by family allowances has led to many protests.
In some letters I have received from families with three, four or five children, it is said that it is no use doubling family allowances if nothing is paid for the first and second child. Anyway, they say, it would be the same.

living, which is always on the increase, we could render a very great service to our large Canadian families.

Some studied historian may one day be able to pinpoint the week end upon which Canada became a major ski power. An unstudied guess, however, would have to be the first week end of last April.
One week before the Crystal Mountain meet in Washington, the Americans had done poorly against the relentless racers from France, Switzerland and Austria. So they went on to the National Alpine event hungry for a chance at redemption. Then somebody let the Canadians onto the course, and for the Americans it was a Bay of Pigs on skis.
And wasn't I pleased.
With stunning suddenness, the Americans faced a new threat. It was almost as if a fifth column had struck secretly from within while American attention was focused on European racers.
Nancy Greene swept the slalom, the giant slalom and the downhill that week end. Rod Hebron pulled a third in the slalom and coach Dave Jacob's skiers were scattered throughout the top ten positions.
The men's slalom at the national was only the beginning. In the national, Rod Hebron, Bob Swan and Peter Duncan all placed higher than the nearest American. In the next three slalom races on the circuit, the best Canadian placed higher than the best American.
Meanwhile, Nancy Greene had hit her stride. She won the two giant slaloms, a qualified first in a downhill, fourth in a slalom and one disqualification in a slalom after a run which was a full second faster than her nearest competitor.
The Canadian team which had gone to the U.S.A. as country cousins returned to Canada as serious contenders for world skiing honours.

Mr. Chairman, I hope this is the correct vote under which to raise a question which has to do primarily with medical services to native Indian people. I want to mention two or three points to the minister. In British Columbia we have a means test type of medicare program and native Indian people who make application for coverage under that program are advised that they are not eligible to be covered because their medical coverage falls under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada. I think this matter was raised a few years ago. The policy with respect to coverage for native Indian people in British Columbia was that if it was considered that the individual had sufficient funds to pay his own medical bills they fell on his shoulders but if it was determined that the individual did not have sufficient funds to pay his medical bills then the department paid them.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
In other words, there was a means test in application then in the case of native Indian

people who cling to what I might call their aboriginal right and feel that the cost of their medical coverage should be borne automatically by the federal government. This feeling is perhaps stronger in British Columbia than elsewhere because in British Columbia the native Indian people have not signed any treaties with respect to their lands. They feel that the Crown, having invaded their territory and exploited resources formerly exploited by the native people, has a concomitant responsibility toward them. They feel rightly or wrongly-rightly, I think-that coverage is the responsibility of the government and should not be dependent upon the application of a means test.
If this is still the policy of the federal government, and from what has been said I believe it is, we find the native Indians in British Columbia facing two means tests. First, there is the means test approach which the federal government has imposed on them for some time. Second, if they want to apply for coverage under the British Columbia medicare plan they find themselves confronted with another means test, a means test which amounts to a prohibition because the attitude of the provincial government is: We want nothing to do with you because you are a federal responsibility. As a result the native Indians find they are covered by no one so far as medical care is concerned.
I wonder whether the minister would care to reply and give an account of the policy of his department in this area. Perhaps he could tell us whether any steps are being taken to overcome the difficulty which native Indians are experiencing in getting medical coverage.
At the same time he might tell us what the situation is with respect to the so-called medicine chest case in Saskatchewan. A year or so ago a court found that the present day application of a provision in one of the old treaties meant that these people should receive medical coverage from the state.

At this moment it is quite evident that we have to ask ourselves whether there is co-ordination in the work of the department, whether there is a meeting of minds and also whether the different branches of the department are directing their efforts to the same cause when they are studying the feasibility of projects and undertaking studies. It seems that the equilibrium has been upset somewhere along the line and I should like to say more about this a little later.
It seems to me we are not heeding the danger signs of inflation in the nation and if we are we are not applying the solutions all across the country. Some areas of the country have been declared as designated areas because there is high unemployment and a great deal of available labour. It seems to me that the measures we are using in this regard are not being applied elsewhere in the country and I hope that the people in the department are aware that domestic measures must be taken to curtail the dangerous inflationary trends. I hope they also realize that an appraisal of government spending programs must be made so that priorities can be applied to certain projects with others being postponed.
Duff Roblin, the premier of Manitoba, tried to impress upon the government some time ago that we could not afford all the requirements of government at once but that priorities must be set in order to deal with them in turn as we can afford them. Many of the projects included in the estimates now before us have not been started. We have items in the present estimates for projects which are of grave necessity but which have been postponed for a number of years.
A few moments ago I suggested there was not a meeting of minds concerning some of the projects which have been undertaken. Before coming into the house yesterday I read an article which appeared in Le Soleil, edition du Bas St. Laurent, concerning port facilities being built in the area of Gros Cacouna. I understand this project will cost in the neighbourhood of $4 million. We are now endeavouring to find out how we are
March 8. 1966

going to utilize these facilities. In the article there is this statement in French:

The decision to make an operational survey of those harbour improvements should also be announced shortly. The survey would be conducted by a specialized firm.

This project is practically complete but we are now going to undertake the study of a portion of it. Does that mean that the branches of the department that studied the project before it was started did not consider all the factors or that there have been changes in the plans of certain individuals who wish to establish industries in the area, or does it mean that this project was simply built to answer the wishes of the people of the area?
The hon. member for Riviere du Loup-Temiscouata is not in his seat at the moment but I want to assure him that I have no objection whatsoever to this project. I do object, however, to the fact that many projects of a more pressing nature have not been proceeded with yet. I think of many small repair jobs that have to be done to wharves and small necessary dredging jobs which would cost from $200 to $2,000.
There seems to be some confusion in this regard. When it comes to these small but necessary jobs they are not proceeded with but when it comes to jobs costing millions of dollars they go ahead. This seems to be a pennywise and pound foolish policy. I refer to the inshore fisheries of the lower St. Lawrence and eastern Quebec. The fishermen there cannot carry out their operations because of sand which has moved into the entrances of the harbours. They must wait until high tide before they can get into or out of the harbours. The dredging of these harbour mouths would entail very small expenditures. It seems that the powers that be get around to doing these small jobs in the month of November after the fishing season is over. When spring arrives the same situation exists because the sand has been carried in again and the fishermen cannot get out to the fishing ground. I know of 25 instances of this kind.
In this same regard I cannot help but think of many slipways which have been built. I trust that professional engineers had nothing to do with the planning of these slipways. Some of these slipways have been built with a stone or concrete wall four feet higher than low tide and I should like to know how a fisherman can get his boat up on the slipway
Supply-Public Works at low tide. There are eight or ten such slipways in my area alone.
On the other hand, I can think of areas where wharves are necessary for the deep sea fishing fleet but because of the lack of repair ships are not able to approach these wharves. There is a lack of bumper facilities, rubber or otherwise, for the protection of these ships. In many instances there are large nails protruding and ship owners refuse to use the unloading facilities. These jobs require small expenditures but they are very essential to the fishermen in the area.
Without taking too much more time I want to refer to the Chandler project and the study which was made by the research council in 1959. This project was proceeded with because of the urgent necessity of having a new harbour at Chandler. In that area there is a pulp mill. One paper machine has been installed and I am sure a second one will be installed in the near future. The company in the area cannot operate efficiently or profitably by using the present facilities at Chandler. The government has asked the company to contribute a certain amount of money toward the project. To date the company has refused to make this money available because of certain conditions which have been imposed. Apparently the contribution amounts to $525,000 payable in two instalments, one of $50,000 and one of $475,000 upon completion of the project. What hurts the company concerned is the fact that the $475,000 is an amount of money which the Department of National Revenue says the company will not be able to charge against operating expenditures.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I have never heard, and I doubt that too many people have, of a case where a private company has been asked to contribute a large amount of money to a capital expenditure for a project belonging to another body or person. In this case the new installation will be the property of the government or the public and the company will be asked to contribute a large amount of money which it cannot deduct from its expenses. I think we have a new approach in this regard and I should like to suggest that the company would accept additional wharfage charges or rental charges involving large amounts of money because they would be able to charge these expenses against their operating costs. In this way the amount of money asked from the company by way of a capital expenditure would in the period of a few years be doubled.

I would therefore ask the minister to endeavour to settle this case as soon as possible because the situation is urgent. I hope that necessary repairs to facilities will be carried out as soon as possible next spring so that those people who wish to work may do so. We should encourage people to work and they should be given the opportunity of pursuing their trade without great difficulty.
We wanted to speak about the tendering system employed by the department. We also wanted to speak on the question of awarding contracts on a regional basis up to a limited amount of money. However, we will delay our discussion of these matters until the estimates for the next fiscal year are before the committee.
As a final request of the minister and the government I ask that a little initiative and perhaps imagination be used in building across this country in maritime areas marinas for those who wish to travel by boat on their holidays. I am sure it is important to these people to know that when they are at sea they can use these marinas as resting places and to obtain protection from the elements of nature. Marinas are needed in the St. Lawrence and gulf areas; they are needed on the lakes. I am sure that with our centennial year approaching many American tourists will be coming to Montreal by yacht and it would be unfortunate if disasters occurred because of the lack of marinas along the St. Lawrence up to Montreal.
