Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure there is a tendency to wish to discuss on a regional basis the proposals made recently by the Department of Public Works. However, I think we should perhaps wait until the minister's estimates for 1966-67 are before us. I am in agreement with the proposition that even though we have not authorized in a technical sense the payment of money for the operations that have taken place under the Department of Public Works, eleven twelfths of the money has been expended and payments under contracts must be made. I do not think that at this late date we shall renege with regard to the operations that have been undertaken in the last year.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that has been drawn to my attention quite forcibly in the last few weeks. It concerns a change in the practice of

the department to which I as a member of parliament am opposed. I have looked at the list of staff members of the department to see how many executive secretaries the minister has because every time I write a letter to the minister or the department I receive a reply from an executive secretary saying that what I am inquiring about cannot be done.
I do not know what qualifications are necessary for one to be an executive secretary but some of the problems I have referred to the department are of a highly technical nature. I have been asking the department for advice whether a project is feasible and have received the reply that the project will not be undertaken. In my opinion it is not for executive secretaries to say whether a project is to be undertaken and in most cases I am not asking for this type of advice but for one of the officials of the department to decide whether it is feasible. As a member of parliament I am asking for this information.
I know this system is adopted in other departments when requests are made of an official and I can see some merit in it in that members of parliament are supposed to deal with these matters at a certain level. However, I believe the Department of Public Works is a pretty broad organization and it is also a fairly technical organization in many aspects of its duties. For this reason I suggest strongly that unless the executive secretaries are Solomons they should leave it to the heads of the various departments to decide whether something can be done.
The matter that I raised with the department was a very simple one and referred to a particular type of soil. My inquiry was whether this soil could be used in greenhouses and, if it could, would it be possible to lease a certain portion of land from the government? I received a reply saying that the government had decided they needed this land and were not going to lease it. There is no point in leasing it if the material is of no value. We can negotiate for the land after it is decided whether it is valuable. My request was for technical advice.
No doubt the minister is well aware, after listening to some of the speeches that have been made previously, that in the field of public works there are wide ramifications. There are highly trained and highly skilled people in his department and I believe that members of parliament can benefit from the advice these people are able to give. When it comes to a matter of policy I agree that this
March 8, 1966	COMMONS
should come from the minister but the system of channelling letters from a member of parliament through the minister's executive secretary is one that I believe the minister himself does not agree with and as a member of parliament I disagree violently when my inquiries are subjected to this delaying type of tactic. Under this practice the suggestion is that the answer is given from the top, which is not necessarily the place at which you wish to start. Therefore I suggest that if this is a new policy, and I am informed it is, it should be discontinued.
There is one other matter I should like to mention, Mr. Chairman, and it was mentioned by the hon. member who spoke before me. I refer to changes that have taken place by regulation. One such change has bothered me because it was an issue in the last election campaign. It was a decision of the Prime Minister to make a change in the harbour facilities for pleasure craft. We have always been interested in knowing why the government had not moved into the field of providing services for this changing environment, particularly on inland waters. I live by a body of water that is a boundary between two provinces. This area has had considerable commercial activity in years gone by but that commercial activity has now changed. While the activity is no less commercial and in fact the volume, moneywise, has increased, it has completely changed. We were interested in the change that could be made by regulation at the insistence of the Prime Minister while visiting British Columbia. He had the opportunity then of involving himself with the yachting society in the area, taking a trip and finding the facilities not suitable. We are all well aware of the fact that the facilities are not suitable in many areas.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
This is something to which the federal government should give consideration. I am surprised that this was done for political purposes. I hope the minister intends to give the house before long some indication of what is the government's intention in this regard. I believe that in every province in Canada tourism is a growing industry. Some aspects of it in some areas are international and in other areas interprovincial and really not the responsibility of the provinces, but no jurisdiction has yet been established in regard thereto.
The minister will probably have to reconsider the regulation which was passed in response to the generous gesture of the Prime

Supply-Public Works Minister but which I think has not been thought out too well. If that is done, then assistance and technical advice can be given areas which will benefit from it in the provision of the proper type of harbour facilities, thus projecting the trend which has developed over an extended period of time.
These are only two considerations to which I should like the minister to pay attention. I hope that when the estimates of the Department of Public Works are brought before parliament in the next few weeks they will be referred to the committee for detailed study because I believe it is a department which affects every member of parliament and we have got bogged down because of the way we have been handling estimates in the past. I want to point out to the minister that he is more anxious to see his estimates passed than to comply with the suggestions and the requests we submit to him rather often.
I wish to call his attention to the Rouyn post office in the riding of Villeneuve. A few years ago, before I came to this house, this post office was enlarged. Now, this extension gives the impression that, instead of a post office in Rouyn, we have some kind of a henhouse.
It should not be overlooked, Mr. Chairman, that the city of Rouyn is the metropolis of northwestern Quebec. It is the largest city and the nerve centre from the economic, social and every other point of view, of northwestern Quebec.
We have very nice post offices in Val d'Or, Malartic, Noranda, we have small post offices in Cadillac, Duparquet, and Evain in the riding. I sometimes wonder what architect in the Department of Public Works had the idea of building a henhouse to serve the population of Rouyn.

March 8. 1966
Supply-Public Works
This post office should be completely done over. And if the minister ever went through Rouyn, he must have seen this shameful building there. The most populous city of the county and of all northwestern Quebec.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) asked me to make representations to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith), so that changes may be made to give us a post office which not only looks like a post office but which meets the needs of our city of Rouyn.
I know that the estimates which we are studying will not allow him to enlarge or improve post offices, but he could use those for the fiscal year 1966-67 to see that the exterior or appearance of the Rouyn post office is changed. It is a sorry sight as it now stands.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like to point out to the minister the pressing need of two airports in our region, one at Val d'Or, the other at Rouyn. In the case of Val d'Or, the necessary credits have been voted and the Minister of National Defence will probably attend to it. In the case of Rouyn, the Minister of Public Works will have to see to it.
All we have now is a small shack, 20 by 24. Fifties of people go to the airport to catch the plane. We have been asking for an airport for at least four years, but the minister has turned a deaf ear.
Another thing:	people from different
municipalities, in that part of the province, of the country, have asked the federal government to help with the construction of wharves on certain lakes in our region. They were told every time: "Since it is intended for tourist purposes, we are not really eager to build those wharves."
I remember, for instance-it may have been about 15 years ago-that under the Liberal administration here in Ottawa, and the present Minister of Public Works sat in this house at that time, authorization had been given for the construction of a wharf at Taschereau. The name was not Taschereau then; the area was known as Pontiac county, but, at Taschereau, a wharf had been built in the middle of a field, approximately 300 feet from lake Robertson. The wharf is still there today and people go there to fish in blue hay, where the water is about six inches deep. They fish for small perch.
This wharf, built with public funds under a Liberal government, is useless, except for a few young people who like to go fishing. As a matter of fact, this wharf is so far from the lake that I wonder whether the minister was
(Mr. Caouette.)
not asked to build a lake along the wharf in order to justify its existence. I wonder.
At any rate, I sincerely believe the minister should give some thought to the building of wharves along certain lakes in the Duparquet area, for instance, an ideal spot for tourists which attracts thousands of persons every year from the United States and everywhere.
People who arrive at the lakes with their fishing gear and a boat are disappointed by the lack of wharves and ramps in our area, and they cannot enjoy their holiday. The Minister of Public Works should heed those requests and authorize the construction of wharves in our area.
Mr. Chairman, these are a few comments I had in mind. I know the minister is anxious to have his estimates passed, but I would ask him to be slightly more anxious to reply when we ask him something. It is all very well to say yes, yes, yes but something must be done.
We cannot be satisfied for ever with "yes" and promises. It may be more difficult to pass the 1966-67 estimates than those we are studying now. Let the minister ask his officials to accede to the legitimate requests not only of the people of my county but also of other counties.
I wish to insist particularly on the building of an appropriate and nice looking post office in Rouyn, so that the one which we have now can be demolished.

Mr. Chairman, normally this is the time when each member should have the opportunity, and take the opportunity of raising questions of a local character respecting the administration of the Department of Public Works in his constituency. I am not going to do that this afternoon. I am going to confine my remarks, and even those will be brief, to the policies of the government, and in particular to the administration of public works on what I would consider to be the national scale.
First, Mr. Chairman, I should like to impress on the officials, and on the Minister of Public Works, that there are a large number of people across the country who feel that the federal government is not following through with the terms and the intent of the Trans-Canada Highway Act that was passed in this house. I think if you were to examine that piece of legislation, it would be found that it was not the intention that the federal government should give only one payment to
March 8. 1S66

the province, as a share of building the highway in the first place. The intention was that Canada should have at least one highway from coast to coast built to sufficient standards to accommodate the requirements of traffic on that highway.
I suggest to the minister as well that the specifications that were called for in 1950, or thereabouts, for a highway across Canada have changed substantially since then. Yet there has been no indication from the government that it intends to continue to assume the responsibility of the federal government to see that there is a modern highway from one end of Canada to the other. The government simply made a payment, I believe in the first place on a shared cost basis of 50-50, and when that highway was completed across any province that was the end of the federal responsibility. Mr. Chairman, we do not accept that as being in keeping with the intention of the Trans-Canada Highway Act.
On looking back you may see many occasions where the federal government has in fact amended the provisions of the Trans-Canada Highway Act by moving forward the completion date, and also changing the federal government's share of the cost of the balance of the unfinished highway, if you like. The result has been that some provinces which were very conscientious and very swift to proceed to build this highway across areas for which they were responsible have in fact been penalized.
We had a debate in the house respecting this matter a few days ago when, I believe, the hon. member for Gaspe introduced a notice of motion respecting some aspects of it. I am not going to talk at any length now, but I believe that there is a need to advance the standards respecting the highway to meet the needs of highway traffic. The federal government should not withdraw from that responsibility. A particular section I have in mind at the moment is a stretch of approximately 70 to 80 miles, from Calgary to the border of the Banff National Park. In view of the Alberta department of highways decision to construct a two-lane highway in the first place, there has been a failure in its capacity to take care of traffic using it.
It has been suggested that when the provincial government proceeds to upgrade the standards of that highway to four lanes, the federal government will refuse to pay a part of the cost of increasing the capacity of the road to meet new traffic conditions.
Supply-Public Works
Mr. Chairman, without taking a great deal of time, I think that the federal government should announce that it intends to participate on a continuing basis in the keeping up to modern standards this highway across the country.
I think, too, that the federal government should change its attitude-if I may use that word-with respect to the disproportionate share that has been paid to some provinces which have been able to delay the completion of the highway.
Participation has moved from 50 per cent to 75 per cent, and in some cases to as high as 90 per cent. We think that this is discriminatory and that it should be changed.
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take time to go into some of the other details, although as I said at the outset, I think this is the appropriate time to do that. I will not do so, because we are in the last month of the fiscal year.
I hope that the minister is ready to give some favourable response to the requests which have been made of his department, that the federal government should not withdraw completely from its responsibilities in keeping up to modern day standards this highway from one end of the country to the other.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments along the lines which have been made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat with regard to, first of all, the Trans-Canada Highway, what to me has become an entirely inexcusable, discriminatory treatment of various provinces with regard to the completion of the Trans-Canada Highway. It seems that those provinces which dragged their feet either intentionally, or otherwise, got the better treatment. Those provinces particularly the western prairie provinces, which completed their construction early were discriminated against. It is true that in that part of the country it is a good deal easier to build roads than in other parts. Surely, they are entitled to the same percentage contribution as some of the other provinces, in so far as the Trans-Canada Highway is concerned. I think what has happened is entirely wrong. I think that the prairie provinces should not have been penalized.
I want to underline what has been said by the hon. member for Medicine Hat with regard to the section between Calgary and Banff. On the one hand we have the government support of the application of Canada for

March 8. 1966
Supply-Public Works the winter Olympics of 1972 which will require an expansion of the road facilities between Calgary and Banff. This notwithstanding some of the bureaucratic nonsense which has come out of the department of northern affairs where some of the senior officials seem to think that it is their duty as administrators to determine when the point of saturation has been reached in the usage of our national parks.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
This is nothing less than bureaucratic arrogance. Our national parks are for the enjoyment of the people. The trans-Canada route was designed to lead to the majority of the national parks in the Rockies, and it is incumbent on us to develop the roads to them but not to penalize the provinces. I think that with regard to this section of the road, the province of Alberta is entitled to additional contributions, in the same way as the province of Newfoundland receives a higher rate, some 75 per cent in respect to the highway. In the same way as the province of Quebec receives particular contributions toward trans-Canada highway construction because of Expo. In addition to that Quebec receives a lot of fringe benefits, if I may call them that, with regard to highway construction in and about the city of Montreal.
I do not understand why there should be this discrimination-and it is rank discrimination. I think a great deal could be said in this same vein on behalf of the province of British Columbia. I wish to draw the attention of the minister to this matter in no uncertain terms. We shall be back dealing with this question time and time again during consideration of the estimates for 1966-67. This is an injustice which must be redressed.
The other point on which I should like to speak briefly tonight concerns the re-organization of the minister's department. It has now become a service department. We want to hear a great deal more about this reorganization than the minister has told us. I have become aware of certain tendencies which might be disquieting. There may be a logical reason for them, but we should have an explanation. Are we to have a series of little empires with planning sections, tendering sections and so on, with "big Father" in Ottawa still looking over the shoulder?
Is there to be a diminution of function here in Ottawa or is this to be merely a proliferation of administrative layers? We must have a detailed explanation. I do not expect we

shall get it tonight but we shall look forward to hearing one at the earliest opportunity.
While the Department of Public Works is engaged in this business of decentralization into the five regions, it is curious to note that some of the other departments seem to be reversing this tendency and are doing away with the co-ordination which is inherent in a regional directorate. I think it is right to allow more authority in the field, but let us consider what other departments are doing in this regard. I have a suspicion that they are missing the boat. As I say, I hope there will be a full and frank disclosure of what has been done in the Department of Public Works, and that an explanation of this new philosphy will be given us at the earliest possible date.

I should like to refer briefly, perhaps "for home consumption", as the phrase is, to two or three communities which are affected by decisions of the minister. These are the communities of Hartley Bay, Kincolith, Kitkatla and Kitimat.
I have had correspondence with the minister about the needs of these communities in recent days. The need of each one of them is the same, namely, a harbour or breakwater system to protect the fishing boats and the people who live in these communities.
The case of Kitimat is a particularly grievous one because an amount for the construction of a breakwater or harbour system at Kitimat had actually been set aside in the estimates, or, if it was not in the estimates as
March 8, 1966

such it was contained in the advance planning provisions or whatever is used by the department to suggest that a certain project is to be carried out almost immediately.
During the period around election time in 1962, funds were on the point of being set aside for the purpose to which I have referred. A decision has been made to proceed with the construction of a breakwater and boat harbour at Kitimat, but it was wiped out by the austerity program which immediately followed that election. Since then it has not been restored.
It was always my assumption, that these projects were placed on a list which was reviewed at least annually so that the correct priority could be determined. It would seem to me that if a decision was made at least three years ago to slate a project for construction, and if this decision was cancelled because of a national emergency at that time, it should have been reinstated at the first opportunity following the end of the emergency. The emergency has been over for a long time now. For this reason, the absence from both this year's estimates and next year's estimates of any provision in respect to this particular boat harbour is particularly grievous. I understand it has been set down for some time in 1967-68. I ask the minister to have somebody in his department advance this particular project as far as possible. Let us see whether it cannot be carried out during the current calendar year or during the current fiscal year.
The needs of the other communities I mentioned are no less urgent. They are all visited by strong winds in the fall, winter and spring. There is no protection to speak of in any of them from southeast gales. The people who live in these places have made fairly large investments in fishing boats, and these vessels need the protection which harbours and breakwaters would afford, o (7:20 p.m.)
I would, therefore, ask the minister to look into this question and give it priority so that the necessary work can be done. I do not mean by this that it be done in 1967-68 but that it be done during the coming fiscal year by way of supplementary estimate, which is the only possible way since the main estimates have already been tabled.
I also wish to make a brief reference to the national capital commission item. Hon. members from the Ottawa area may think it is a bit presumptuous for someone from 2,000 or
Supply-Public Works 3,000 miles away to comment about our national capital in the manner which I propose, but quite frankly I think the highway and road system in the capital is a ruddy disgrace. Many people who come to Ottawa express this point of view. They are shocked at the condition of the streets, especially at this time of year. The potholes that develop, seemingly in a matter of minutes are a disgrace to the national capital.
During the daytime I see people out in the streets filling in these potholes with hot asphalt, or running a hot iron over them, but they must be working in two shifts. They must go out again at night and dig them out, because next day no one would notice any change. This goes on year after year after year. Every spring it is the same blessed thing. To put it bluntly, the roads here are a disgrace to Canada and to the national capital.
At this juncture I am not particulary concerned whose responsibility it is, but we do have a National Capital Commission and I presume one of its functions is to beautify the national capital, to make it a pleasant place in which to live, and a pleasant place to visit. But with the potholes and the roads the way they are, it is a deterrent to people enjoying themselves and having a pleasant time driving around the city while they are in Ottawa.
I understand that a few years ago somebody sponsored a pothole contest. I do not know if it is still in existence, but you could win a prize by pointing out the biggest pothole of the week. Somebody once turned in a whole city block but they ruled his entry out because they thought that was going too far.
Somewhere along the line this situation has to be altered. I know there was conflict between the National Capital Commission and the city hall over some of these questions but surely to heavens, if we have any pride in our national capital, we should do everything we can to find ways and means to improve these streets because, in this modern age of motor vehicle transportation, their condition is something which affects everybody.

Mr. Chairman, only ten months before the centennial year one would anticipate a major discussion on the National Capital Commission estimates. It is only because of the mood of the committee tonight that I refrain from engaging in such a discussion, but I do point out to the committee that not since 1961 has there been a genuine discussion of the National Capital Commission estimates in this house. In fact, I think there has been only one speech made on the subject since 1961. Since 1955 there has not been an examination of the activities of the commission by a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. So I am going to ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works to reconsider the proposal I made earlier during this session, that the estimates and the activities of the commission be referred at this session to a joint committee for study.
Mr. Chairman, I did not make that proposal for the purpose of seeking an investigation of the commission. Quite to the contrary, I made it to give the commission the opportunity of having its fine story heard and to indoctrinate the members of this house, who must vote the money for this National Capital Commission, with regard to the fine work that is being done. If the minister does not

agree to my proposal to send these estimates to a joint committee, I suggest he make a major presentation at this session, before the standing committee on Crown corporations, or the standing committee on housing, urban development and public works. If he will do that, it will be exceedingly useful.
In order to prepare the national capital for the centennial year I believe a crash program is urgently needed. By reason of the lack of co-ordination between municipal and federal authorities, the Department of Public Works and the National Capital Commission, the central part of this national capital last year was an unholy mess.
I think we must make absolutely certain there is co-ordination, and that we have a crash program to prepare the capital for what we hope will be a wonderful celebration only a matter of months from now.
My hon. friend, the member for Skeena, took his usual pot shot at the potholes in the city of Ottawa. I should like to say to him that many of those potholes are the result of the neglect of this parliament during the past 15 or 20 years in depriving the taxpayers of Ottawa of the moneys that were properly due. If there are these potholes today, it is because of that lack in days gone by. I hope this lack will be made up, and that under the fine leadership of the hon. member for Ottawa West we will have a crash program to prepare the capital as it should be prepared for the centennial year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like, while we are studying Secretary of State estimates, to draw the attention of the minister to a problem about which she is aware. Ever since 1962, we have repeatedly pointed out to the government and the Secretary of State the problem which exists in my riding, the Chapleau riding, with regard to broadcasting and television in the cities of Chibougamau and Chapais.
At the present time, radio and television networks cover practically the whole country; over 90 per cent of all Canadians have access to these services, but there are still some centres, cities in Canada, where there is no television and radio.
That may not be exactly the case for Chibougamau and Chapais, for the citizens of these two municipalities do have television, thanks to a cable and microwave system.
These people are served, but they must pay a fortune to get television signals, while the organizations of both these municipalities have already, on several occasions, submitted briefs and resolutions to the Department of the Secretary of State and to the government with a view to obtaining the same radio and television service as every other Canadian region.
I have here the last of the resolutions submitted recently to the Department of the Secretary of State asking that these services be provided without charge, as they are in every other part of Canada.
This brief, submitted by the Chamber of Commerce of Chibougamau was endorsed by the local public bodies, namely the municipal corporations of Chibougamau and Chapais, the Chambers of Commerce, the Labour Unions and the Owners' League, in short, the whole population of these two cities.
The brief submitted recently read as follows:
Whereas, on several occasions, requests were made to the C.B.C. and to the Department of Transport to get free television in the region of Chibougamau-Chapais, and that such requests never produced anything;

Whereas the cities of Chibougamau and Chapais are remote cities which pay practically the highest taxes because of their geographic location;
Whereas the cost of living in our region for gas, groceries, etc., is higher than elsewhere;
There is no doubt that, in a region very remote from other centres, the transportation costs increase, thus lowering considerably the purchasing power.
I now resume reading the resolution:
Whereas most salaries in Chibougamau and Chapais come from the mining industry and are therefore higher than in other regions, they bring more money into the public treasury;
Whereas we are not asking for more than the others around us are getting but that we are asking for at least what we are entitled to;
Whereas there are approximately 15,000 people in Chibougamau-Chapais and that we are happy to say that our region does not live off the government, the spectre of unemployment does not exist in our part of the province;
It is quite true; as soon as someone becomes unemployed, the cost of living is so high that he cannot stay long and has to leave.
I continue:
Whereas television in a Canadian home is no longer a luxury but just a means of information, entertainment, culture, etc. and that it becomes a necessity and a right which is ours as it is everywhere else in Canada, and without charge;
Whereas in the larger centres colour television will soon be available to all and that it should at least be given in black and white in our region;
I wish to point out to you, sir, and to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) that the people of Chibougamau and Chapais are not asking to stop preparations to give colour television to the other regions but at least that television in black and white be given to
them.	They are not asking for what belongs to others but only for what belongs to them.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
I go on:
Whereas, at present, some people can afford black and white television with poorer results than elsewhere and by paying the following prohibitive prices:
First, a television set costs more than elsewhere, secondly, the sizeable sum of $200 must be paid for the connection with the community antenna and
then,	a fee of $7 a month of $84 a year, plus a 6 per cent provincial tax that other areas do not have to pay;
And they can only get one channel. But if they do not pay that amount, they are without any television at all.
Whereas the only benefit in living in an area such as ours is that we can earn our daily bread, while the handicaps are many such as:
1. Gravel roads that easily wreck a car within the first 30,000 miles.

2.	Gasoline at 12 cents a gallon more than elsewhere;
3.	Fuel oil 3 cents a gallon more than elsewhere with heating required twelve months a year;
4.	Being further away, we have to use the telephone service more often than elsewhere, and this is anything but free;
5.	Transportation of all materials increase substantially the cost of living in our area;
6.	Electricity costs about twice as much as elsewhere plus 6 per cent additional in taxes.
7.	Rents are higher than elsewhere;
8.	Building costs are higher because of transportation and the tax on materials;
9.	The great distance from large towns is detrimental to the education of our children beyond a certain level.
For all the reasons listed in this brief, which is a positive statement of the plain, definite ideas of the people of Chibougamau and Chapais, we urge the authorities concerned to study this brief seriously and to answer us, not by ambiguous statements, but by immediate action.
The Chamber of Commerce of Chibougamau.
That, as I said earlier, was endorsed by all the public bodies and the people in Chibougamau and Chapais.
On many occasions, Mr. Chairman, I myself asked the previous Secretary of State to correct that situation I was told that we had to wait until the Fowler report on broadcasting was presented. We have now had this report for several weeks, several months even. But the government does not seem too much in a hurry to implement its recommendations.
Mr. Chairman, what I want to point out to the minister is the fact that the people of those two towns are the victims of a serious injustice on the part of the C.B.C.
And here, I submit to the Secretary of State that the Fowler commission put the finger on what is happening to those people. As a matter of fact, on page 68 of the report, it is said:
All Canadians pay for the national broadcasting system-not just for the C.B.C., but for the whole system, including the private radio and television stations. They pay for about a third of the total cost when they pay their taxes. They are paying for the other two thirds every time they run around to the corner store for a can of soup or a loaf of bread. Many of them are thus paying for broadcasting services they cannot enjoy. Clearly, much remains to be done.
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is the case with regard to the people of the cities of Chibougamau and Chapais, they pay for services which they do not enjoy. That is unfair and the government must not tolerate this situation any longer. It must immediately order that the C.B.C. be given the necessary
Supply-Secretary of State funds to enable it to extend the radio and television services not only to Chibougamau and Chapais but everywhere in Canada where it is physically possible to do so at the present time.
A little further, on page 83 of the English version of the Fowler Commission report, these words struck me:
Therefore, during the next five years, a firm degree of restraint should be applied to the licensing of new stations, public or private, taking the real need for broadcasting service, radio or television, into account.
It cannot be denied that the needs are obvious as far as isolated centres are concerned. They need those services for entertainment, culture and information.
On page 83 of the same report, it is said:
We believe that, for the next five years at least, the formula now being used by the C.B.C. to determine the eligibility of communities for television service (2,000) or radio service (500), either in English or French or both, is sound.
However, we are not satisfied with the planned rate of expansion to meet the needs disclosed by the formula; we think that, given the necessary approval and financial provision, it could and should be accelerated;
It means that the government should put at the disposal of the C.B.C. the sums needed for its expansion to enable it to serve the people who are not yet getting any service.
The recommendations follow:
1.	That, during the next five years, no new C.B.C. stations should be opened in centres that now have service as determined by the formula presently used for eligibility.
2.	That consideration be given to the feasibility of accelerating the rate of progress now planned by the C.B.C. for extending coverage, both radio and television in English and French, to centres eligible for public service under the formula.
Mr. Chairman, in the light of these recommendations, the government is no longer justified to hesitate and it must accede immediately to the request of the towns of Chibougamau and Chapais with regard to radio and television services.
On page 124 of the Fowler report, I notice another paragraph in which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation says how it conceives the mandate it has received from parliament:
Whether Canadians live in remote or heavily populated areas, the national system should serve them as adequately and equitably as possible.
This suits very well those areas and I invite the minister to study carefully the resolution that has been submitted to her and to give a very special and immediate consideration to these legitimate requests. I am
March 8, 1966

Supply-Secretary of State
convinced of this and I am sure the minister is also.
When C.B.C. officials are asked whether it is materially possible to achieve these purposes, they answer yes, but that the government does not make sufficient funds available to the Corporation, suggesting it is too costly at present to serve those areas.
As far as the Chibougamau-Chapais area is concerned, it is served by private enterprise at present, as I said earlier, but at a prohibitive price for these people. Out of the 2,400 or 2,500 families living in this area, at least 1,000 are unable to afford these services which are provided free of charge everywhere else.
So, C.B.C. officials tell us that their policy is to give a perfect signal in any area served. Well, Mr. Chairman, what the citizens are asking for immediately is not so much a perfect signal; as a matter of fact, they would be quite satisfied with what they have at present provided it would be free of charge as anywhere else in Canada.
Consequently, I suggest to the hon. Secretary of State, that she invite the officials of the C.B.C. to meet representatives of private enterprise which actually serve the area, as well as representatives of the two cities to come to an agreement. It would cost less to the C.B.C., expenses would be less than they are now and the service supplied to the two cities could be improved gradually. I am sure this would give the whole population, which has been waiting for a long time, the same service that can be found elsewhere in Canada.
So, Mr. Chairman, I hope the Secretary of State will consider the recommendations I have suggested to her tonight. A delegation of about 15 people from that area came to Ottawa today at their own expenses, which is quite a sum. They have not come here for the fun of it, but to see that justice is done, and I am convinced that the Secretary of State can render this delegation immediate justice.

speechtext:
Without too much fanfare, and I might say without too much criticism, the present government authorized the C.B.C. to make expenditures on colour television. I can assure the hon. lady and the corporation that there will not be too much criticism from unserviced areas about launching a program of colour television, because the people in those unserviced areas know that we must face up to progress. However, it is difficult for them to understand why-and I think the government now must accept this-if money is available for colour television, it is not available to provide service to other areas now unserviced. I do not intend to be unkind when I say that each year as we have looked over the C.B.C. estimates covering some millions of dollars, we do not see too much of a breakdown of how this money is to be spent.
I realize that the corporation puts out an annual statement, which is widely distributed. In that annual statement there is a breakdown to some extent of the manner in which this money is spent. However, it always amazes me when I see, looking at vote No. 1 under the corporation, the words:
Grant in respect of the net operating amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service.
It shows $96,799,000. Mr. Chairman, there are 18 words in that explanation which works out to approximately $5 million a word. I would have hoped the C.B.C. could have added three more words, something like "extension of service" because at $5 million a word we would have enough money to provide service to all of the people who are not as yet receiving this television service.
In the report of the corporation for 1963-64 it was pointed out that according to present planning it would take something over ten years to bring service to those areas which are now unserviced.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
The sum of approximately $15 million would be needed. Many years ago I asked officials of the corporation whether the corporation would consider approaching parliament for a special grant of money to enable them to finish the job. It was felt by the
Supply-Secretary of State corporation at that time that parliament, unfortunately, would not be very receptive to a request for a special grant of this nature. Year after year no request was made. But in the annual report of 1963-64, the corporation did make this suggestion. I noticed with interest and pleasure that in the most recent annual report the corporation makes a similar request. In this instance, however, the corporation recommends that specific grants to the corporation should be made by parliament for this purpose. They say this was the procedure followed in the initial stages when radio was brought to the north under similar economic conditions. The corporation says it believes television to be an amenity which could do much to make life in the north more attractive and help the development of our frontier areas. The point here is that the corporation is recommending that parliament provide this special grant of money sufficient to enable it to finish the job of extending television services.
The corporation, as I understand it, has recommended that parliament provide sufficient funds to enable it to go into colour television. One of the questions which I believe the government should answer tonight is this-How was the decision made as to which of these recommendations was to be carried out? I believe it is important that the people in areas such as I represent get an answer to this particular question. In my constituency, at least, the many thousands of people who are interested in receiving this service are not greatly critical about the advent of colour television. What they say is this: if Canada can have colour television we can also have the extension of service.
I notice that the corporation has recently extended services into the Jasper area of Alberta, or else it is planning to do so. Services were extended recently in the area east of Kenora, Ontario. The people in my area look at these things and ask: how many are being served, and what does it cost? They want to know these things so that they may be in a position to decide whether any discrimination is being shown in determining which areas should be served first.
I have discussed this matter carefully on many occasions with officials of the corporation. Time and time again, we have gone over the formula which the corporation is using to determine which areas should be serviced. They use a cost per household formula. They tell us that in a certain area people can be served for $7, $8 or $10 per household, and
March 8. 1966

Supply-Secretary of State these people will naturally be getting service earlier than those where the cost may be as high as $15 per household.
I suggest that the use of this formula leads to discrimination, and I should like the Secretary of State to convey to the officials of the corporation the reason I believe this is so. In the most recent annual statement of the corporation we find the cost of production and distribution of television services in Canada amounted to a total of $91,863,839, almost $92 million. This is the amount which was required to service about 92 per cent of some four and a half million households in Canada. But suppose for the moment that this $92 million is servicing all the four and half million households in Canada. This is the figure which should be used, in all fairness when making these calculations. We would then arrive at the amount it is actually costing the corporation.
I say it amounts to discrimination when the corporation looks at the areas which are still to be served and says: We shall work on a figure of $4 or $5 per household because that is what it costs us to put television into one particular area. The cost should be figured on an all-Canada basis in order to be fair.
These figures can be juggled in a number of ways. When I look at this $92 million for the cost of production and distribution of television services, servicing 92 per cent of four and a half million households in Canada, I find that this works out to an average across the nation of some $20 per household. This is the basis on which I feel the corporation should look on further extensions. It all boils down to the fact that the extensions will take money. We are all agreed on this. I think the government of the day should at least make up its mind to tell the people in these areas whether or not it is prepared to grant a sum of money to the corporation sufficient to do the job.
Many times during the last session of parliament I asked the Secretary of State whether the government was considering providing such a sum. On each occasion I was assured by the Secretary of State that the government did not intend to consider any specific grant of money to the corporation until the Fowler report had been received.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
But before the Fowler report was received by the government some $15 million was provided for the corporation to allow it enter the colour television field. I do not see how we can get along quickly with these estimates

unless the government can give us a satisfactory explanation for doing that, and tell us when it will provide the money which the corporation says is necessary to service these areas.
The information which the corporation officials give us is helpful on many occasions, and what I have to say is not in criticism of them, but they tell us that within the next five or six years Canadians will have their television service bounced from satellites orbiting the earth. This is certainly feasible from an engineering point of view, but people in areas which are still unserviced are reluctant to sit back and wait for this to happen when they know that within the next 18 months the C.B.C. could acquire sufficient equipment to service their areas. All the C.B.C. needs for that purpose is a grant of money from this parliament. I also believe the corporation has an obligation to tell these people when it plans to service their areas.
Many of the people in these areas would be a lot happier if they knew they could get television reception in two or three years. The corporation should be able to determine the time it will take.
People in the northern Manitoba area who receive fringe reception from private stations carrying C.B.C. programs, or who may have the benefit of a cable system operated by private enterprise, are told by the C.B.C. that it cannot make application to enter the area because it is already serviced. Consequently, there would be duplication of services. The corporation does not say this in quite those words, but it feels the licensing authority would be reluctant to allow it to do so. It is probably quite right. The C.B.C. already has made application to go into the city of Saskatoon, but I understand that its application is being held up; I suppose temporarily, although I do not know.
However, I can recall that a few years ago the C.B.C. application to go into the city of Edmonton was granted. There was a public hearing at which those wishing to complain were able to do so. But the C.B.C. application was granted, and if ever there was duplication of services that situation in Edmonton was it at the time of the application, the city had ample T.V. service from private stations.
I said I was not going to cover the subject of programming, but with the advent of colour television more questions need answering. I noticed that the other day the Maple
March 8, 1966

Leaf Garden Corporation estimated that colour television would provide it with something like $9 million revenue from the program it has on the air within the next three years. I do not know how much profit there is for the C.B.C. from "Hockey Night in Canada" but it is certainly a popular program. Most viewers want to see it continue, but in view of the estimate made by the corporation sponsoring Maple Leaf Gardens I only hope the C.B.C. will get its fair share from that program.
The area in northern Manitoba which is asking for immediate service has a population of some 100,000 people. A considerable portion of the area already receives television service from the Yorkton station which carries C.B.C. programs. But I think I am quite safe in saying that if, in the first place, there had not been a hassle between the C.B.C. and the B.B.G. that area of Manitoba would have been available to the C.B.C. for network programming. However, it is still available, except that we are told there is no use in the corporation making application to service it since it is already serviced. But I repeat, that is exactly what happened in the city of Edmonton.
The part of the area surrounding Flin Flon and The Pas has been serviced with cinescope programming, films being delayed one week, and the picture reception is good. But there are some 20,000 people in that area who feel the time is long past when they should be receiving the network service.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If you take the 100,000 people from Dauphin through to Flin Flon and on to Snow Lake, who are asking for this programming at the present time, they come well within this cost per household which I mentioned. I know the corporation can say there are other areas which they can service at a cheaper cost per household, but I think the figure they should use is the figure of $20 per household which you get when you look at the amount it costs to service the number of households which are being serviced in Canada.
Quite often one hears comments in respect of the advisability of a member of parliament rising to criticize the corporation for what it is or is not doing. I do not think this is the case, but I have been told that when one rises in the House of Commons and starts criticizing the present system of priorities, the area that one represents may find itself a long way down the list.
Supply-Secretary of State

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should like to thank the committee for allowing me to continue. I was about to say I would not like this committee to get the idea that this is any threat which has been passed on to me through anyone connected with the C.B.C. This is not so. However, I hear this in my area. I am informed that if we continue to criticize, we may have to wait a long, long time for this service. I think the government can straighten this matter out in short order, if they will assure this committee they are receptive to the suggestion and are willing to provide this sum of money which the corporation already has recommended in its annual report. Then everyone would be quite happy.
I will be quite surprised if this is not a lengthy discussion, because we are told by the corporation-and I do not doubt their figures-that there are some 50 areas in Canada which remain to be serviced. So, if there are 50 other areas which are as anxious to get this service as is the area which I represent, then I would imagine we are going to have quite a long discussion, unless we receive an answer from the government.
I did not mean that I was speaking for all those other areas; I was merely referring to all the places which were not serviced. I have noticed, Mr. Chairman, on the many, many occasions when I have risen in this house to speak about television, that it always seems to me this is a subject in which perhaps not too many people are interested. I suppose mainly this is because most of the areas which the members represent already are serviced. However, one time during the hearings of the broadcasting committee a few years ago I mentioned that if there was any threat that the Grey Cup, for instance, would not be televised in Canada, every member of this house would be up on his feet howling his head off.
Strangely enough, about a year later, it appeared as though the Grey Cup was not going to be televised. If you think we have had some crises in this house during the past few years, just recall what happened on that
March 8, 1966

Supply-Secretary of State occasion. The house was in an uproar for a full day and it continued on spasmodically for the rest of the week, until somebody intervened, I understand, and the matter was resolved. This is the reason I say that the people who already have these services should realize what it means to the people who do not have them. If one of your favourite programs is discontinued, you are ready to howl. However, probably it is not too interesting to hear someone discussing the need for television.
I will listen, Mr. Chairman, with interest to any of the members who have problems similar to ours, in their areas which are not serviced. I think we should have several answers from the government or from the corporation. In relation to the areas which are still without the service, I think we should be told by the corporation what areas these are and where they are.
Also, I think we should be told what the priorities are for each of these areas at the present time in the C.B.C.'s planning. I recognize, as I said before, that it is difficult to expect the corporation to lay down a list of priorities and expect that those priorities will remain the same the next year or the year after; but I think we are entitled to know what priority each of these particular areas has at the present time.
I believe the main question we should have answered by the corporation is, on what date will each of these areas be provided with C.B.C. television service. As I mentioned, the government could eliminate the necessity of these questions being answered if they would assure the committee that they are prepared to see that a sufficient sum of money is provided so that the C.B.C. will be able to do this work immediately. This answer to that question will satisfy the people in all of these areas. I am hoping, as the debate progresses, that we will receive an answer to some of these questions from either the Secretary of State or from the corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I want to speak briefly concerning C.B.C., and more particularly on the housing conditions, namely, the building in which the C.B.C. operates while there are prospects of interesting sites offered by the municipal authorities.
The present situation in Montreal is becoming more and more permanent and it requires a rapid solution, because it is so

obvious with regard to administration. In fact the C.B.C. operates 17 different offices scattered almost everywhere in the city of Montreal from one end to the other; this, of course, leads to lack of co-ordination and to increased and repeated expenses which the C.B.C. could avoid.
It also puts the artists in a very awkward position. Under the present circumstances, they must, on very close and often crowded schedule, for some of them, run around the city to take part in various broadcasts. Accordingly, they have to turn down certain jobs because of the geographic situation.
It must not be forgotten, on the other hand, that Montreal is the artistic capital of Canada, and that the C.B.C., reflecting as it does a major part of the arts in Canada, should therefore be well served.
How can we solve that administrative breakdown, as far as premises are concerned?
The city of Montreal has offered the C.B.C. a plot of 27 acres. It gave the undertaking that it would clear this land, unfortunately located in a ward with many slums. The city of Montreal fulfilled its obligations; it cleared the land and tore down the slums. But the government delays its decision to have the new C.B.C. building built as soon as possible. The city of Montreal had put the deadline at October, 1965 for the start of construction, but today, we are still waiting for the first shovelful of earth to be taken up.
The grouping together in the same building in Montreal of all the services of the French and English networks of the C.B.C.-and everybody agrees on this, both C.B.C. authorities and the Fowler commission-would be a very good thing, and it is urgent.
From the administrative point of view, when the execution of a project is delayed, someone must take the consequences, and that someone is always the citizen who pays taxes, because of slow administration.
This is a field in which the government has had time to think, plan and act. The government is still taking its time and so risks losing the land placed at its disposal by the city of Montreal. This land was to be used before October 1965; it is now March 1966 and nothing has been done yet. It would be surprising if the city of Montreal were to wait indefinitely. This is why I think it is urgent that the minister and the cabinet make a decision, especially since Expo '67 is drawing near and this land, so rare in Montreal, is situated near the Expo grounds.
March 8, 1966	COMMONS
It would be unwise to keep unused indefinitely this piece of land located on Dorchester boulevard. If we want to show that Canada is prosperous, we must not leave a hole right in the middle of a city. Besides, it would be interesting to see to what extent, if not the government, at least the owners of old houses surrounding the C.B.C. square, would be willing to improve the district as soon as possible, so that the slums would vanish from the city that we are going to show to the world.
If we really want to live the motto "Man and his world", it is not enough to display it in a window, but to have it at home, to build it at home, in every street, in every district, in short in every city and in every province.
Before closing, I wish to say, simply from the administrative point of view, that, in my opinion, the Fowler commission and C.B.C. are again in complete agreement on this point; in fact, the Fowler commission raised the same problem in the city of Toronto. Therefore, an administrative problem does exist that the Corporation would like to see settled, that the Commission wants to see settled, but that the government, unfortunately, is in no hurry to solve, although it should do so as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, all the agencies for which the hon. lady is parliamentary housekeeper appear to be under discussion on item 1 of her estimates. Therefore, although the committee is desperately crowded for time, I make no apology for insisting upon an opportunity of dealing briefly but explicitly with what has become a very highly sensitive, indeed, an explosive issue in the public service, namely the inept and improper handling by the government and the Civil Service Commission of the problem of bilingualism. Precipitate and ill considered attempts to change the ground rules for promotional and other competitions are leading to discrimination against French speaking and English speaking civil servants alike, and to widespread discord throughout the civil service. Action taken surreptitiously and clandestinely by the Civil Service Commission, only partly revealed in an indiscreet speech made by the chairman of the Civil Service Commission on February 1, has placed the whole merit system in jeopardy and flouted the Civil Service Act.
An unfortunate, indeed, unbelievable statement of future recruitment policy by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys has
DEBATES	2407
Supply-Secretary of State intensified the problems, and an attempt made by the Minister of Public Works to pour oil on troubled waters has not been effective.
Sir, this is a very delicate problem where one may easily be misinterpreted. I seek only to bring justice to all civil servants, whether of French speaking or English speaking derivation, and I shall try to choose my words carefully and with moderation, although there is no doubt that the time has come to call a spade a spade and to appeal directly to the Prime Minister to stop the erosion of one of the greatest public services in the world.
I welcome the Prime Minister's announcement this afternoon that there will be further consultations with civil service staff associations, and I hope those associations will truly reflect the opinions of their members. For, sir, it is useless to blink at the fact that there is greater anxiety, more uneasiness, unrest and subdued anger in the civil service in Ottawa at this moment than at any time in my memory.
What is happening, sir, and I want to make it clear, is that in my view the civil service commission has confused job requisites, in which bilingualism is a most significant factor, with principles of personnel rating and evaluation, in which it has no place.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Because of that, the merit system is being outrageously flouted. I say that the whole basis upon which Canada has built the finest Civil Service in the world is in grave jeopardy. The Civil Service Act was completely revised by this house as recently as 1961, and it is clear and explicit as to job requisites. Section 47 of the act reads this way:
The number of employees appointed to serve in any department or in any local office of a department who are qualified in the knowledge and use of the English or French language or both shall, in the opinion of the Commission, be sufficient to enable the department or local office to perform its functions adequately and to give effective service to the public.
Those, sir, are the tests as to whether a job is to be bilingual or whether it is to be unilingual. These tests were agreed upon without complaint in a special committee of this house as recently as 1961, although there was some resistance in the house itself by the hon. member for Hull and the hon. member for Sainte-Marie. But the tests, I suggest, are twofold; first, adequacy of performance of departmental functions and, second, to give effective service to the public.
March 8. 1966

Supply-Secretary of State
No one can complain legitimately when the application of these tests results in the specification of a bilingual officer or the specification of a unilingual officer whether that unilingual officer be French or English. But when those tests of job requisites are falsely and improperly imported into the evaluation or rating of the merit of an individual to hold a job, which job does not require a knowledge of two languages, then I say the time has come to expose this fallacious reasoning.
Section 38(1) of the Civil Service Act is the enunciation of the merit system which has stood unbreached since the days of Sir Robert Borden, the father of the merit system. I want to put the words of that section on record, sir. They are:
The Commission shall examine and consider all applications received within the time prescribed by it for the receipt of applications and, after considering such further material and conducting such examinations, tests, interviews and investigations as it considers necessary or desirable, shall select the candidates who are qualified for the position or positions in relation to which the competition is conducted, and shall place them in order of merit.
We cannot play with words, Mr. Chairman. Merit is merit, not merit plus 10 per cent for some factor extraneous to merit which the Civil Service Commission chooses to import into the plain meaning of the word in violation of that plain and natural meaning. There is in the Civil Service Act one explicit departure from the merit system, the introduction of the veteran's preference. The mere fact that there is a statutory exception to the merit principle is a clear indication that there is no other. Section 33 is equally clear. It reads:
The Commission may in relation to any position of any class or grade prescribe qualifications as to age, residence or any other matters that in the opinion of the Commission are necessary or desirable having regard to the nature of the duties to be performed, but in so doing the Commission shall not discriminate against any person by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion.
In other words, the Commission has the power, and in proper cases the duty, to prescribe bilingualism as a job requisite, but it has no authority to discriminate when it comes to evaluation and rating of individuals on the basis of merit. Yet, what has it done? The chairman of the Civil Service Commission made a speech on February 1, 1966, in which he made the following statement:
The Commission has recently recognized proficiency in the two official languages as an element of merit in selection for appointments and promotions to positions in the National Capital area and

in other centres where the public being served is sufficiently representative of the two cultures of Canada ... In these cases, proficiency in the two official languages is considered as an additional asset and is accorded 10 per cent of the total selection rating score.
Well, sir, this speech and this procedure I say first flouts directly the will of parliament and is in contempt of parliament. Why do I say that? On September 19, 1961, as appears in Hansard at page 8573, the hon. member for Hull moved an amendment to add subclause (2) to clause 47 as follows:
At the time of competitions, those candidates who can establish that they possess a sufficient knowledge of the two official languages of Canada shall benefit by an added 5 per cent over all other candidates-
You find at page 8575, Mr. Chairman, that this amendment was negatived by a vote of 43 to 16. Yet in the face of that vote and without any further consideration by parliament, the Commission expresses its contempt of this house and institutes the very procedure this house rejected-it institutes it two for one. If this is the policy of the government now, there is a clear duty on the government to come back to this house and stake its life upon the adoption of a policy already so clearly rejected by the house.
This speech of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission was the first announcement that, surreptitiously and without the knowledge of any of the staff associations, a 10 per cent advantage had been put into effect in the national capital area and in other centres of Canada for those with proficiency in the two official languages. This 10 per cent, I submit, will be an effective barrier to unilingual candidates in most competitions, whether knowledge of two languages is necessary or not for the performance of their duties. Very rarely indeed in a competition is there such a wide margin between candidates, and the result is that tens of thousands of civil servants who entered the Civil Service under one set of ground rules will find their advancement or promotion blocked and barred. Frustration, dead-end, blind alleys -these will be the lot of thousands.
The introduction of this 10 per cent preference into the merit system is in my view without colour of right. It flouts completely, as I have submitted, the structure of the Civil Service Act. It is within the prerogative of parliament to do this; it is not within the prerogative of the Civil Service Commission. If parliament chooses to do this, it is one thing, but for the Commission to do it I say drives a horse and cart through the whole
March 8. 1366

merit system and discriminates equally against French speaking and English speaking civil servants. I emphasize that it discriminates against French speaking and English speaking civil servants alike. I say, Mr. Chairman, that it will lead to the demoralization of the civil service and will make a farce out of bilingualism.
I tell the committee that if it had been in effect in 1927, it would probably have deprived the Department of External Affairs of the services of one Lester B. Pearson. If it had been in effect later, I doubt whether the [DOT]civil service would have had the dubious advantages of the services within its ranks of the now hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate or the hon. member for Eglinton. Actually, Mr. Chairman, one of the major problems is to define objectively what is in fact bilingualism. Many people who profess to be such are truly not. Some objective standard, I submit, must be devised. Thirty years ago I was reasonably bilingual, at least to the extent of being able to make numerous speeches in the French language. Lack of opportunity has deprived me of any proficiency in that respect. Yet others scarcely more proficient than I claim to be bilingual.
This 10 per cent rule, I point out, will prevent promotions from other centres of Canada to the national capital.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
No longer will it be reasonable for a postal worker, a customs or immigration officer to expect promotion from Regina or Fort William, from Ville Marie or Rimouski, from Halifax or Saint John, to the headquarters of his department in Ottawa. Practically, an officer in these places cannot be bilingual. He cannot practise the other language to keep up his proficiency, and he cannot expect to circumvent the 10 per cent preference. The net result will be that the future civil service of Canada will be drawn from the very tiny group or segment, only 12.23 per cent of the population according to the last census, who speak both French and English. I repeat those figures, there is only 12.23 per cent who speak both French and English.
Eliminated from the civil service of their native country will be the 19.13 per cent who speak only French-almost 20 per cent of the people in the country who speak only French -as well as the 67.35 per cent who speak only English and the 1.27 per cent who speak neither. Within the present civil service, promotions will be confined to a select inner few made up of only a tiny percentage of the
Supply-Secretary of State total service. The fact is that the members of the Civil Service Commission themselves could not qualify today under the rules that they themselves have laid down.
Let me be clear, Mr. Chairman. Where the job requires a knowledge of the two languages, as many jobs do, of course, in order to provide proper service to the public under section 47, I believe that that must be clearly laid down as a job requisite. But to breach the merit system by an artificial, unrealistic percentage will set back rather than promote the cause of bilingualism. I have it confirmed in writing by the chairman of the Civil Service Commission that this 10 per cent rule is now in effect in all areas of Canada which have an English or French mother tongue minority of at least 10 per cent.
It is not easy to say these things, sir. It is very easy to be interpreted as being antiFrench. I have spent a large part of my life trying to bridge the gap which exists in this country. But as an Irishman, sir, I am neither anti-French nor anti-English. I seek tonight to be a Canadian interested in the welfare of the 87 per cent of my fellow Canadians, French, English, and other ethnic groups alike, who do not enjoy the undoubted advantage of bilingualism.
I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works is not in the house at this moment, for between us, the minister and I represent over half the civil service population. I make a direct appeal to the Minister of Public Works as a man of moderation, as a man of tolerant understanding, as a man of firmness and of character, to use his prestige and his moral stature within the government to reverse the unwise policies which have been embarked upon, policies which will do injury to French speaking, English speaking and other Canadians alike.
I say to this committee tonight, let us not completely stultify the best civil service in the world. Let us not permit the public service of Canada to founder upon illusory rocks which can only endanger the unity of the nation. I ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works to protect the civil service of Canada. If they fail in their duty we shall have a mass exodus of technical and professional personnel to the United States, to Australia and to New Zealand, which will do permanent injury to Canada. This cannot be permitted to happen, sir.
I ask every member of this house, French, English, or whatever their ethnic background, and I do so with the greatest sincerity at my
2410	COMMONS
Supply-Secretary of State command, to rise and to protect the greatest public service in the world from that which is being done to it.
